The Republic of Benin (Benin) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter), which it ratified on 20 January 1986.

In accordance with the provisions of Article 62 of the Charter, Benin submitted its 6th to 10th Combined Periodic Report on the implementation of the provisions of the African Charter (2009-2018) on 27 August 2020.

The report highlights the developments recorded in the country in the promotion and protection of human and peoples' rights, as well as the legislative, administrative and judicial measures taken in the implementation of the provisions of the African Charter for the period 2009-2018.
The Combined Periodic Report was examined on 19 and 20 November 2021, during the 69th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission).

The report was presented virtually before the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) by the high-level Beninese delegation, led by Mr Jacques Kodjoh, Deputy Secretary General of the Ministry of Justice and Legislation.
It should be noted that the report received and examined by the Commission related only to the implementation of the provisions of the African Charter.

The Commission notes with satisfaction the 2019 constitutional revision in Benin, which enshrined, among other things, the abolition of the death penalty and the promotion of the representation of women in the National Assembly.

At the normative level, the Commission welcomes the adoption of several legislative texts relating to the promotion and protection of human rights by the Government of the Republic of Benin, from 2009 to date.

At the institutional level, the Commission takes note of the reform of the Autonomous Electoral Commission, the operationalisation of the Beninese Human Rights Commission, the National Institute for Women and the Central Office for the Protection of Minors, the Family and the Suppression of Human Trafficking.

Nevertheless, the Commission remains concerned about a number of issues, on which it makes recommendations to the Republic of Benin, regarding the measures necessary to strengthen the enjoyment of human rights, as guaranteed by the Charter, the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), as well as other relevant regional and international instruments. The African Charter - Article 62: Obligation to submit reports

The Commission takes due note of the 6th to 10th Combined Periodic Report on the implementation of the provisions of the African Charter (2009-2018), submitted by the Republic of Benin on 27 August 2020.
Benin's commitment, which means it is now up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter, is to be welcomed.

However, the Commission notes with concern that the present report relates only to the implementation of the African Charter. Recommendation: the Republic of Benin should include in its next periodic report, in addition to the part devoted to the implementation of the provisions of the Charter, a second part dedicated to the Maputo Protocol and a third to the Kampala Convention, ratified on 13 October 2005 and 28 March 2012 respectively. -

The Commission takes due note of Benin's ratification, during the period under review, of several international human rights instruments, both at the level of the African Union and at the level of the UN.

However, the Commission remains concerned about the non-ratification of several other relevant international instruments. Recommendations: the Republic of Benin should: - Continue its efforts towards the ratification of the: Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa, Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security, The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. - Within the framework of the reforms undertaken, reconsider its decision to withdraw its Declaration under Article 36(4) of the Protocol to the Charter establishing the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights. - Article 1: legislative measures for the domestication of the provisions of the African Charter

The Commission welcomes the adoption of several legislative texts relating to the promotion and protection of human rights by the Government of the Republic of Benin from 2009 to date. Recommendation: the Republic of Benin should continue its efforts to domesticate the provisions of international human rights instruments, in particular by completing the adoption of the laws on associations, trafficking in persons and human rights defenders. • Law No. 2021-12 on sexual and reproductive health, • Law No. 2021-11 on Special Measures for the Suppression of Offences Committed on Grounds of Sex and -

The Commission adopted two resolutions on the human rights situation in Benin, in 2019 and 2021 respectively, with recommendations to the Beninese authorities to ensure the application of the provisions of the African Charter in the management of the pre- and post-election demonstrations that the country experienced between 2019 and 2021.

The Commission notes with concern the adoption of Law 2019-39 of 7 November 2019, granting amnesty for criminal acts, misdemeanours and minor offences committed during the legislative elections of April 2019. Recommendations: - The Republic of Benin should give greater importance to the implementation of the Commission's recommendations aimed at ensuring the application of the guarantees of the African Charter in all circumstances and, in particular, avoid the adoption of laws seeking to restrict their enjoyment. - Benin should grant compensation to the victims of the acts classified as crimes, misdemeanours and minor offences committed during the legislative elections of April 2019. - Article 26: National Human Rights Institution (NHRI) and other institutions
The Commission congratulates the Beninese Human Rights Commission on obtaining affiliate status during the 69th Ordinary Session held in November / December 221.

The Beninese Human Rights Commission submitted its application for accreditation to the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) in 2021. Recommendation: the Republic of Benin should provide the Beninese Human Rights Commission with the financial and human resources necessary to fully carry out its mandate as a National Human Rights Institution. - Article 2: Right to non-discrimination
The Commission takes note of the efforts to empower women and to promote their representation in elected bodies.

However, discrimination may be based on other factors, in addition to that based on sex (between men and women). Recommendation: Benin should consider adopting a comprehensive anti-discrimination law to cover all the factors that may serve as a basis for this phenomenon. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Prisons, Conditions of Detention and Policing in Africa - Article 3: Right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law - Article 6: Right to liberty and security of the person and protection from arbitrary arrest - Article 7: Right to a fair trial

The Commission takes note of the creation of the Benin Prison Agency and the increase in the annual budget allocated to it. The Commission also takes note of the National Policy for the Development of the Justice Sector launched in 2014 and of Law No. 2020-08 of 23 April 2020 on the modernisation of justice, with several innovations, such as the establishment of some new courts, better observance of the rule of reasonable time, the introduction of a procedure for the settlement of small claims and the creation of the information office for litigants.
In 2009, the Commission had recommended that Benin ensure the training of judges and other officials on the protection of human rights.

The Commission noted in the report submitted and in the interaction that took place during its presentation that it is not clearly indicated that the State Party has an initial and continuing training programme for law and security officials. To this issue is added the integration of the instruments adopted by the Commission, in particular the Luanda Guidelines, the Guidelines on Policing Assemblies and the Mandela Rules.

The Commission noted that in Benin, the minimum age of criminal responsibility is 13 years, but that there is no formal educational programme for minors in detention, that is, minors in conflict with the law. Recommendations: Benin should: - Strengthen the guarantees of persons subject to trial in the context of the ongoing revision of the Code of Criminal Procedure. - Continue efforts to improve conditions of detention. - Strengthen the use of conditional release and alternatives to imprisonment. - Integrate teaching on the protection of human rights into the training programmes of law and security officials, in particular those drawn from the instruments adopted by the Commission, notably the Luanda Guidelines, the Guidelines on Policing Assemblies and the Mandela Rules. - Put into practice in penitentiary institutions the principles contained in regional and international documents on the detention of minors in conflict with the law, in particular educational and vocational training programmes. - Ensure the training of judges and other officials on the protection of human rights. Mandate of the Working Group on the Death Penalty and Extra-judicial, Summary or Arbitrary Killings in Africa -

The Commission reiterates its congratulations to Benin for the abolition of the death penalty in law and the ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty. The abolition of the death penalty is now a constitutional principle enshrined in Article 15 of the Constitution. Benin is the champion State at the continental level in the abolition of the death penalty. It was the first country to host the First Continental Conference on the Abolition of the Death Penalty in 2014. The declaration that concluded this Conference (the Cotonou Declaration) recommended to African States, among other recommendations, to support the draft Protocol to the African Charter on the death penalty.
The Commission takes note of the commutation of the death sentences of 14 detainees to life imprisonment in 2018.

In 2009, the Commission had recommended that Benin finalise the steps towards the abolition of the death penalty. Recommendation: - As a champion abolitionist State, Benin is invited to continue its contribution to regional and international efforts towards the universal and effective abolition of the death penalty, by publicising and sharing its national experience in this regard. - Support the Draft Protocol to the African Charter on the Abolition of the Death Penalty, in accordance with the Cotonou Declaration. Mandate of the Committee for the Prevention of Torture in Africa - Article 5: Prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment

The Commission takes note of the efforts undertaken by the Government of Benin to combat torture, in particular the existence of a National Mechanism for Compensation for the Consequences of Acts of Torture and Related Acts, but nevertheless remains concerned about several shortcomings, in particular with regard to the definition of torture in Articles 523 and 465 of the Criminal Code and the absence of a National Preventive Mechanism. Recommendations: Benin should: - Accelerate the amendment of the Criminal Code, in particular to include a definition of torture. - Establish a National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture. - Strengthen the capacities of the National Mechanism for Compensation for the Consequences of Acts of Torture and Related Acts. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa - Article 9: Right to receive information and freedom of expression

The Commission takes due note of the information contained in the report on the decriminalisation of press offences. It also takes note of the Government's statement specifying that the Information and Communication Code in force in the Republic of Benin is aligned with the Commission's Model Law on Access to Information in Africa.

In 2009, the Commission had recommended that Benin review its legislation to decriminalise press offences and ensure better protection of journalists against arbitrary arrest and detention. Recommendations: Benin should: - Provide, in its next reports, more details on the media landscape in the country (media statistics: print, audiovisual, private, public, etc.). - Ensure the full implementation of the guarantees relating to access to information, in particular those included in the Information and Communication Code and the Digital Code. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders in Africa and Focal Point on Reprisals in Africa - Article 10: Right to freedom of association - Article 11: Right to freedom of assembly

The Commission takes note of Article 25 of the Beninese Constitution, which enshrines the freedom of demonstration and assembly, as well as the existence of draft laws on associations and human rights defenders.

However, the Commission remains concerned about the provisions of the law on "amnesty for criminal offences" committed during the violence linked to the demonstrations that followed the parliamentary elections. Recommendations: Benin should: - Take into consideration the relevant regional and international standards, such as the Commission's Guidelines on Freedom of Association and Assembly in Africa, in the process of revising the law on associations and adopting the one on human rights defenders. - Consider applying a notification regime for the holding of peaceful demonstrations in place of an authorisation regime, and decriminalising acts relating to "the organisation of, or incitement to organise, an unauthorised demonstration". - Strengthen the dissemination by law enforcement officials of the Commission's Guidelines on Policing Assemblies by Law Enforcement Officials in Africa. - Article 13: Right to participate in the conduct of public affairs

The Commission takes due note of the adoption of Law No. 2019-41 establishing the Charter of Political Parties, Law No. 2019-43 establishing the Electoral Code, and the establishment of the Permanent National Electoral Council. Recommendation: the Beninese Government should take all necessary measures to ensure that the forthcoming elections proceed smoothly, in a peaceful and democratic climate.

The Commission is concerned that the State Party, in drafting the Periodic Report under review, did not follow all the guidance contained in the document: "Guidelines for State Reports on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (Tunis Guidelines)". Recommendation: the Beninese Government is invited to follow the Guidelines for State Reports on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (Tunis Guidelines) when preparing its future periodic reports. - Article 14: Right to property

The Commission notes with satisfaction the Government's initiatives to improve access to land ownership for rural communities through the rural land certificate and the provisions of Law No. 2013-01 of 14 January 2013 on the Land and State Property Code, guaranteeing every natural or legal person of Beninese nationality the right to acquire a building or land in the Republic of Benin. Recommendation: the Beninese Government is invited to continue its efforts to strengthen access to property, without discrimination, and to accelerate the resolution of land disputes. - Article 15: Right to work
The Commission welcomes the Youth Employment Programme, which enabled the Government to reach 17,000 young people, including at least 50% young women.

However, the Commission is concerned by the absence of information on the restrictions imposed on the right to strike in certain sectors considered sensitive. Recommendations: the Beninese Government is invited to: - Continue its efforts to establish a support fund for micro and medium-sized enterprises and to strengthen women's entrepreneurship. - Ensure the promotion of the right to work and access to work in the context of the ongoing revision of Law 98-004 of 27 January 1998 on the Labour Code. - Guarantee respect for the right to strike in accordance with the relevant international standards. - Article 16: Right to health

The Commission notes that Benin adopted Law 2020-37 of 3 February 2021 on the protection of health and is making efforts to regulate the quality of care. The Commission notes the absence of information on the budget allocated to the health sector and its evolution (positive or negative). Recommendations: the Beninese Government is invited to: - Guarantee adequate human, material and financial resources to enable the implementation of the various components of the country's health policy. - Take the necessary measures to comply with the requirements of the Abuja Declaration, which require that at least 15% of the national budget be devoted to health. Continue efforts to improve the rate of health coverage and the rate of attendance at health facilities. - Article 17: Right to education

The Commission takes note of the efforts of the Beninese Government to generalise education at all levels, improve its quality and school conditions, and increase the allocation of university scholarships.

On the other hand, the drop in the school enrolment rate of girls compared to boys, during the period under review, is a source of concern for the Commission. Recommendation: the Beninese Government is invited to continue the efforts and initiatives aimed at combating the root causes already identified of girls dropping out of school at all levels of education. - Article 22: The right to Economic, Social and Cultural Development

The Commission has identified several initiatives launched by the Beninese Government with a view to achieving the economic, social and cultural development of the population, in particular: - The National Micro-Credit Programme, - The National Social Programme, - Insurance for Strengthening Human Capital (ARCH), - The construction of 12,000 affordable social housing units out of the 20,000 planned, - Efforts to strengthen access to drinking water, - Efforts to strengthen food security and control the prices of mass-consumption food products, - The establishment of the Culture Support Fund, - The establishment of the National School Feeding Programme and the allocation of additional resources to canteens.

The Commission's major concern in this regard is the availability of human, material and financial resources for the implementation of the above-mentioned commitments. Recommendation: the Beninese Government should ensure that adequate resources are provided to ensure the effective implementation of the initiatives aimed at consolidating economic, social and cultural development in the country. -
The Commission reiterates its concern about the absence of a part dedicated to the implementation of the provisions of the Maputo Protocol in the Periodic Report under review.

The Commission takes note of the efforts of the Beninese Government to promote women's rights, in particular with regard to combating early and forced marriages and female genital mutilation, the promotion of gender equality in matters of succession, and the adoption of the 2021 law on violence against women.
The persistence of certain traditional practices, such as levirate, widowhood rites and exchange marriages, constitutes an obstacle to the promotion of women's rights in Benin.

The Commission takes note of the efforts to empower women and to promote their representation in elected bodies. Indeed, the low participation of women in public and political life in Benin is another poor performance that should be underlined.

In 2009, the Commission had recommended that Benin promote the participation of women and combat discrimination against them. Recommendations: the Beninese Government is invited to: - Include in its next Periodic Report a third part on the implementation of the Maputo Protocol. - Observe, when preparing the part devoted to the implementation of the provisions of the Maputo Protocol in the next periodic report, "The Commission's Guidelines for State Reporting under the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa". - Continue efforts to ensure the effective participation of women at all stages of the design, preparation, implementation and evaluation of development policies and programmes. - Step up efforts to strengthen women's leadership and the participation of women in public and political life. Mandate of the Working Group on the Rights of Older Persons and People with Disabilities in Africa

The Commission takes note of the 2017 law on the protection and promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Republic of Benin. Nevertheless, it remains concerned about the absence of detailed and up-to-date statistical data on persons with disabilities. Recommendations: the Beninese Government should: - Accelerate the ratification of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. - Strengthen the involvement of persons with disabilities and older persons in the development and evaluation of the policies and programmes developed for their benefit. - Strengthen programmes for the care of older persons. - Put in place initiatives aimed at better integration of persons with disabilities into public life, in particular with regard to accessibility. Mandate of the Special Rapporteur on Refugees, Asylum Seekers, Internally Displaced Persons and Migrants in Africa

The Commission reiterates its concern about the absence in the present Periodic Report of a third part dedicated to the implementation of the provisions of the Kampala Convention, ratified by Benin on 28 March 2012.

The Commission takes note of the efforts of the Beninese Agency for the Integrated Management of Border Areas in issuing identity documents to combat statelessness. Moreover, the Commission is concerned by the lack of information on the number of refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced persons in Benin. Recommendations: the Beninese Government should: - Include in its next Periodic Report a third part on the implementation of the Kampala Convention. - Provide updated statistics on refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced persons in the next Periodic Report. - Guarantee the rights of refugees, in accordance with international standards. - Adopt a migration policy guaranteeing the rights of migrants, in accordance with international standards. - Continue efforts to combat statelessness. - Put in place policies for the protection of internally displaced persons in accordance with the provisions of the Kampala Convention. - Put in place legal and institutional mechanisms, including a law, for the management of internally displaced persons. Mandate of the Committee on the Protection of the Rights of People Living with HIV (PLHIV) and Those at Risk, Vulnerable to and Affected by HIV in Africa

The Commission takes note of Law No. 2005-31 of 10 April 2006 on the prevention, care and control of HIV/AIDS and of the National Strategic Plan to Combat HIV/AIDS and STIs (2015-2017). It nevertheless remains concerned about the increase in HIV prevalence in certain Departments, such as Littoral, Atlantique, Mono and Ouémé.

In 2009, the Commission had recommended that Benin adopt a legislative framework for the protection of persons living with HIV/AIDS, in particular against discrimination. Recommendations: the Beninese Government should: - Address the challenges relating to the implementation of Law 2005-31 of 10 April 2006 on the prevention, care and control of HIV/AIDS, in particular with regard to combating discrimination and stigmatisation of persons living with HIV/AIDS. - Pay particular attention to, and adopt specific actions on, the fight against AIDS in the Departments that record an increase in the prevalence of this disease. - Articles 19, 20, 21, 23 and 24: Mandate of the Working Group on Extractive Industries, Environment and Human Rights Violations in Africa

The Commission takes note of the adoption of the new Petroleum Code and of the detailed information provided by the State under review on the nature and legal framework of the exploitation of natural resources in the country. Recommendations: Benin should - When preparing its next reports, follow the Commission's Guiding Principles for State Reporting on Articles 21 and 24 of the African Charter relating to Extractive Industries, Human Rights and the Environment. - Guarantee better respect for environmental standards in the implementation of the new Petroleum Code. Mandate of the Working Group on Indigenous Populations/Communities and Minorities in Africa

The Commission notes with concern that the periodic report and the responses of the delegation do not provide indications as to the existence of indigenous populations/communities in the Republic of Benin, or as to the status of the ethnic groups called "Baatonu" and "Fon of Benin". Recommendations: Benin should - Put in place laws or measures to raise public awareness and redress any injustices and inequalities that may affect indigenous communities in the Republic of Benin. - Further enshrine, in law as in practice, the recognition of the rights of indigenous communities to own, use, control and manage lands, territories and resources. ***
The examination of periodic reports is an important component of the Commission's mandate.

The obligation to submit reports, which is incumbent on States Parties, is in fact an effective tool for assessing the implementation on the ground of the human rights enshrined in the African Charter.
The Commission wishes to congratulate the Republic of Benin on the submission of its 6th to 10th Combined Periodic Report on the implementation of the provisions of the African Charter (2009-2018).

The constructive engagement of the Beninese authorities during the examination of the present periodic report is also to be welcomed. Benin is encouraged to continue its constructive cooperation and engagement with the African Commission.
The Commission hopes that the present recommendations will be taken into account and implemented by the Government of Benin.
Benin is now up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter.

In accordance with the provisions of Resolution 517 on the method of computation of time limits for the submission of periodic reports ACHPR/Res.517 (LXX): The Commission invites the Republic of Benin to submit its next periodic report (11th Report) on the implementation of the provisions of the Charter, the Maputo Protocol (Initial Report) and the Kampala Convention (Initial Report) in August 2024. The Republic of Malawi (Malawi) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter or the Charter), having ratified the Charter on 17 November 1989.
Malawi also ratified the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights relating to the rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), on 20 May 2005.

Malawi submitted its Initial and Combined Periodic Report to the African Charter to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) at the Commission’s 56 Ordinary Session, which was held from 21 April to 7 May 2015. The Initial and Combined Periodic Report covered the period from 1992 to 2013.
The Report under consideration, covers the period from 2015 to 2019, and combines the second and third periodic Reports (the Report) of Malawi.
The Report was presented to the Commission by the Delegation from Malawi (the Delegation), attached to this Report as Annex 1.
The Report was considered by the Commission during its 68 Ordinary Session held virtually from 14 April to 4 May 2021.

The Report highlights the developments which had taken place in the country, on the promotion and protection of human rights, and measures which had been put in place by the State to comply with its obligation under the African Charter and the Maputo Protocol in the period between 2015 to 2019.

The Commission welcomes the presentation of the Report by Malawi and commends the Delegation for its frank and constructive dialogue with the Commission during its presentation of the Report. In this regard, the Commission wishes to congratulate Malawi, for its diligence and commitment to its obligation under the African Charter and the Maputo Protocol.
These Concluding Observations give an account of the positive aspects, the factors restricting the enjoyment of human rights and the challenges identified in the Report.

In conclusion, the Commission makes recommendations to Malawi on measures for strengthening the enjoyment of human rights as guaranteed by the African Charter, the Maputo Protocol as well as other relevant regional and international human rights instruments. PART A: Concluding Observations and Recommendations on the Combined 2 and 3 Periodic Report of Malawi for the period 2015-2019 under the African Charter I.
The Commission notes a number of positive aspects in Malawi’s efforts towards the fulfilment of its obligations under the African Charter.

The Commission: i. Welcomes the efforts made by Malawi in preparing and presenting its periodic Report and commends the latter for its commitment towards implementing the provisions of Article 62 of the African Charter; ii. Notes and Appreciates that the second and third periodic Report of Malawi indicates the legislative, policy, institutional and other measures which have been taken to implement the Maputo Protocol, in line with Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol; iii. Commends the efforts made by Malawi to ensure that the preparatory process of this periodic Report was highly participatory and involved relevant stakeholders including civil society organisations; iv. Commends Malawi for setting up a National Task Force through the Human Rights Section in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs to coordinate implementation of the Commission’s 2015 Concluding Observations on the Initial and Combined Periodic Report of Malawi 2015 on the African Charter; and v. Lauds Malawi for providing comprehensive answers to the issues raised by the Commission in its Concluding Observations on Malawi’s Initial and Combined Periodic Report (1995 – 2013) 2015, enabling the Commission assess the progress recorded by Malawi during the reporting period, in the protection and promotion of human and peoples’ rights, as well as the outstanding challenges.

The Commission commends Malawi for ratifying the Protocol to the African Charter on the Values and Principles of Public Service and Administration and the International Convention for the Protection of all Persons from Enforced Disappearances during the period under review.

The Commission commends the legislative, policy, judicial and institutional measures adopted by Malawi during the reporting period to enhance the enjoyment of human rights by Malawians, including notably: i. Trafficking in Persons Act 2015; ii. Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act 2015; iii. Court Amendment Act 2016; iv. Land Act 2016; v. Customary Land Act 2016; vi. National Agriculture Policy 2016; vii. National Policy for Older Persons 2016; viii. The Gender Equality Act Implementation and Monitoring Plan (2016 – 2020); ix. National Strategy on Inclusive Education (2016 – 2020); x. The Constitutional Amendment Act 2017; xi. Access to Information Act 2017; xii. National Planning Commission Act 2017; xiii. Health Sector Strategic Plan II (2017 – 2022); xiv. National Action Plan on Trafficking in Persons (2017 – 2022); xv. Accelerating Inclusive Local Governance and Participatory Democracy for Effective Social Economic Development (2017 – 2023); xvi. HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act 2018; xvii. Political Parties Act 2018; xviii. National Action Plan on Persons with Albinism (2018 – 2020); xix. National Strategy on ending child marriage (2018 – 2022); xx. National Strategy for Adolescent Girls and Young Women (2018-2022); xxi. National Disability Mainstreaming Strategy and Implementation Plan (2018 – 2023); and xxii. Citizenship Amendment Act 2019.
The Commission commends Malawi for operationalising the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) in 2020.

The Commission congratulates Malawi for its efforts in safeguarding the right to life including by observing a moratorium on the death penalty since 1994, the abolition of the mandatory death sentence for murder and treason, as well as efforts towards legally abolishing the death penalty for all offences.

The Commission commends Malawi for the: i. Administrative efforts aimed at establishing a complaint handling mechanism in selected prisons in Malawi, to ensure that cases of torture are effectively reported; ii. Various institutional measures adopted to address the issue of overcrowding in prisons such as: iii. reviewing inmate records for early release, holding field courts inside prisons, monitoring and inspecting prisons by the Inspectorate of Prisons, releasing prisoners on bail, acquittal and discharge or order to perform community service and granting of presidential pardons; iv. Establishment of the Lay Visitors Scheme under Sections 124 -126 of the Police Act 2010, which allows members of the community to assess and report on the conditions of detention in police stations; and for v. Steps taken to fully operationalize the IPCC, created under the Police Act 2010 and mandated to receive and investigate complaints from the public against Police officers and the Police Services; to investigate deaths or injuries due to police action; and to investigate all deaths and injuries that occur during police detention.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Regulating Communications services through the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (MACRA) which operates independently of the Government of Malawi (the Government); ii. The sensitization campaigns organized by the Electoral Commission, on the importance of freedom of expression and access to information during elections and how to exercise the rights cautiously so as not to compromise the integrity of the elections; iii. Implementation of the Communications Act, 2016 enacted to ensure that consumers of communications services including internet connectivity are provided with affordable services and that the consumers are protected from any exploitative and prohibitive practices by communications companies; and iv. Efforts made by the Government through various bilateral and multilateral initiatives to ensure that the cost of internet connectivity becomes affordable for the majority of consumers of communications services.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Embarking on the development of a National Migration Policy to ensure coordinated and efficient efforts by relevant stakeholders in the management of migrants. The Policy provides a framework for the safe, orderly and regular management of migrants whilst upholding national interests as well as the human rights of the migrants; and ii. Adopting the National Disaster Risk Management Policy which presents the aspirations of the Government of Malawi in ensuring that disaster losses and impacts are sustainably reduced.

The Commission welcomes: i. The Government’s “I Belong Campaign to End Statelessness in Ten Years (Campaign)” which features a Global Action Plan for 2014-2024 and aims to resolve existing major situations of statelessness, prevent new cases of statelessness from emerging, and assist in better identifying and protecting stateless populations; and ii. Pledges made by the Government at the High-Level Segment on ending Statelessness in October 2019, including undertaking and publishing a qualitative study by June 2020 to better understand the situation of groups and individuals staying on its territory, who are stateless or at risk of statelessness, with a view to finding a solution to their situation as well as review the Nationality/Citizenship Law.

The Commission notes with appreciation the Court Amendment Act (2016) establishing divisions in the High Court of Malawi in an effort to enhance access to justice and improve the efficiency of the judiciary.

The Commission appreciates the establishment of the Legal Aid Fund and welcomes the setting up of district offices of the Legal Aid Bureau, to increase access to justice and ensure legal representation for indigent persons.

The Commission commends Malawi on: Right to housing i. Signing of an agreement for a grant from the African Development Bank to implement the Post Cyclone Idai Emergency Recovery and Resilience Project which aims to reconstruct and rehabilitate damaged infrastructure (including roads, bridges, and water supply and sanitation facilities) and to restore agricultural livelihoods. Right to work i. The enactment of the Employment Act which provides for the minimum age of entry into employment; and ii. Implementation of the Malawi Youth Forest Restoration Programme which provides young people with training and jobs, as well as foster environmental stewardship throughout the country.

Right to health (HIV/AIDs) i. The enactment of the HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act (2018) which prohibits discrimination of any person on a basis relating to HIV/AIDS related infections, and establishes the National AIDS Commission which oversees all issues relating to HIV/AIDS; and ii. The coordinated approach provided in the National Health Policy (2018 – 2030) which addresses key issues central to the development and functioning of the health system in Malawi, particularly: health service delivery; preventive health and social determinants for health; leadership and governance; health financing; human resources for health; medicines, medical supplies, medical equipment and infrastructure; population management; and health information.

Right to education i. Dissemination of the National Inclusive Educational Managers from National Level to Zonal Levels targeting Directors, District Commissioners, District Education managers, Secondary and Primary School Head teachers, and teachers; ii. The establishment of the National Inclusive Education Strategy 2016 to 2020; and iii. The development of a 10 year (2020-2030) National Education Investment Plan by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology which has taken Inclusive Education and Gender as one of its priority areas. Right to water i. Prioritization of water and sanitation activities including the Malawi Growth and Development Strategy III which seeks to provide safe water supply and improved sanitation to people of Malawi including the elderly and vulnerable; and ii.

The Malawi Vision 2063 which also prioritizes water and sanitation as very key in the country’s development. Right to food i. Donation of food and non- food items to assist households that were affected by the Cyclone Idai in collaboration with other Partners; and ii. Adoption of the National Multi-Sector Nutrition Policy (2018 – 2022), which provides a guiding framework for the successful implementation of the national nutrition response and seeks to uphold the Government’s commitment to eliminate malnutrition in all forms. Right to culture i. Adoption of the National Cultural Policy (2015) which aims to identify, preserve, and promote Malawian arts and culture for national identity, unity in diversity, posterity and sustainable socio-economic development.

The Commission welcomes the steps taken by Malawi to address trafficking in persons, through the development of the National Action Plan on Trafficking in Persons (2017 – 2022) which lays out priority actions, including: prevention and awareness raising, victim protection and assistance, legislative framework, policy development and law enforcement.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. The Constitutional amendment under Section 23 (6), increasing the age of the child from sixteen (16) to eighteen (18) years with a view to curbing child marriage and the steps being taken to harmonize all laws on the age of the child; ii. The elimination of child labour, including through: Developing the List of Hazardous Work for Children Order, containing specifications of works that children aged between 5 – 17 years are prohibited from doing; The adoption of the National Code of Conduct and National Action Plan on child labour; and Implementation of various programmes including; Child Labour Elimination in Action for Real Change (CLEAR), and Achieving Reduction of Child Labour in Support of Education (ARISE); and iii. Efforts to address violations of children’s rights, through the development of legal and policy frameworks, including: Child protection and Justice Act, Trafficking in Persons Act, National Policy on Orphans and other Vulnerable Children, National Early Childhood Development Policy, National Social Support Policy, National Education Policy, and the National Human Rights Action Plan.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Efforts taken to protect the rights of older persons and persons with disabilities, including the National Policy for Older Persons 2016; draft Bill for older Persons and the 2012 Disability Act under review; ii. Implementation of the National Policy for Older Persons which adopts a multi-stakeholder approach; iii. The protection of the right to education for persons with disabilities through lobbying for inclusive education; iv. Polices adopted to address issues affecting persons with disabilities including the National Action Plan on Persons with Albinism as well as the National Disability Mainstreaming Strategy and Implementation Plan (2018-2023); and v. Training of sign language communicators to be deployed in courts, including Ministries and the National Assembly.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. The adoption of the Mines and Minerals Act of 2019 which provides a contemporary regulatory framework for the mining sector in Malawi and through the inclusion of several progressive clauses safeguards national interest in contracts that Malawi signs with different multinationals for the harnessing of national resources; ii. The provision on “community development agreements”, which places a mandatory obligation on mining companies to contribute no less than 0.45 per cent of their annual gross sales revenue on community development activities as prescribed in Community Development Agreements (CDAs); iii. The Tree planting campaign rolled out in all districts in the country in 2020; and iv. The launching of the Malawi's Strategy on Climate Change Learning in February 2021 by the Minister of Forestry and Natural Resources, with the objective to contribute to the National Climate Change Resilience Programme through the strengthening of human resources skills development and institutional arrangements for the advancement of green, low emission and climate resilient development.

The Commission notes factors restricting the implementation of the rights enshrined under the African Charter as follows: i. Weak implementation of national laws and policies, which inhibits Malawi’s ability to ensure that all its citizens enjoy the rights guaranteed under the African Charter; ii. Limited resources at the disposal of the State, which has affected progress in the implementation of human rights related programs; iii. Slow pace of institutional reforms to match the constitutional standards and the obligations under the African Charter, which affects the pace of enjoyment and enforcement of human rights in Malawi; and iv. Despite progress in the general awareness of rights in Malawi, there is still lack of public awareness of the human rights among citizens as guaranteed under the African Charter, resulting in a lack of empowered citizens and consequent weak demand for the fulfilment of human rights by the Government.

While recognising the significant efforts made by the Government to promote and protect human rights in accordance with the provisions of the African Charter, the Commission is however concerned about the following:

While the Commission appreciates Malawi’s response to its recommendations in Malawi’s initial and combined Report of 2015, it however notes that, the current Report does not provide specific and comprehensive answers to some of the questions and issues raised by the Commission. In this regard the Report does not for instance, provide comprehensive disaggregated data, including gender disaggregated data on its implementation of the rights guaranteed in the African Charter in order to allow the Commission to objectively assess Malawi’s level of compliance vis-à-vis the obligations contained in the African Charter.
In addition, the Report does not also follow the Commission’s State Reporting Guidelines under Article 62 of the African Charter.

Malawi has not yet ratified some key regional human rights treaties which are critical for enhancing the enjoyment of human rights, including: i. Protocol to the OAU Convention on Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; ii. Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights; iii. Protocol to the OAU Convention on the Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; iv. Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons in Africa; and v. Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa.

Malawi has not yet ratified some key international human rights treaties, including: i. International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families; ii. Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), aiming at the Abolition of the Death Penalty; iii. The Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture; iv. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; v. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; vi. Optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; vii. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure; and viii. Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture (OPCAT).

In addition to the above, Malawi is yet to domesticate some relevant regional and international human rights treaties that it has ratified, notably, the African Charter and the International Convention for the Protection of all Persons from Enforced Disappearance, due to its dual system for domestication of international law under its legal architecture.

The Commission is generally concerned about the lack of information in the Report regarding adequate awareness of the population about their rights, legal procedures and available remedies in respect of their civil and political rights.

The Commission is concerned that: i. Malawi has neither signed nor ratified the OPCAT and there are no indications on the steps taken to ratify the same; ii. Malawi has not expressly criminalized torture under its Penal Code and has not domesticated the UN Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading treatment or Punishment (CAT); iii. The Report does not contain information on measures the Government is putting in place to raise awareness amongst members of the judiciary on their obligation to open inquiries into allegations of torture or ill-treatment particularly when they are raised during trial; and iv. The Report is silent on the remedies that are available for suspects who have been convicted despite alleging that their confessions were obtained through torture.

The Commission is also concerned about: i. The lack of information on legislative and other measures that are in place to ensure adequate redress for victims of torture including compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition; and ii. The lack of definitive data in the Report on the number of victims of torture including on persons with albinism, and measures adopted to ensure adequate redress for victims of torture including compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition.

The Commission is concerned that: i. Malawi has observed a moratorium on the death penalty since 1994.In this regard, while noting the positive steps taken, there remains concerns as to prison conditions for death row detainees, and deaths of persons in prison custody; and ii. Lack of data on the re-sentencing hearings for individuals who had previously received the automatic death sentences in light of the 2007 Malawi High Court Kafantayeni decision, which prevents the Commission from making an objective assessment of the process.

The Commission is concerned about the: i. Conditions of the current prison facilities, as they continue to house inmates of all categories; ii. Lack of data in the report on rehabilitation, recreation and education programs and facilities available to prisoners; iii. Lack of information regarding the number or quality of meals for inmates; as well as information regarding sanitary facilities and the availability of antiretroviral drugs for inmates with HIV-AIDS; iv. Lack of statistics on deaths in prisons and places of detention; v. Lack of information on the continuous training of law enforcement officials in matters relating to the protection of human rights; and vi. Lack of information regarding the number of female Officers recruited in the Police and in the Penitentiary/Correctional Services.
The Commission is concerned that Malawi has not adopted a Refugee Policy and that the National Migration Policy which incorporates aspects of refugees, is still pending approval by Cabinet.

While the Commission appreciates the post Cyclone Idai Emergency Recovery and Resilience Project, the Commission is concerned that this project only targets five (5) out of fifteen (15) districts and two (2) cities affected, resulting to unequal distribution of resources and remedies to the victims in other affected areas.
The Commission is concerned with the fact that the draft Bill for older Persons has not been enacted into law, while the 2012 Disability Act is still under review.
The Commission is also concerned with the lack of disaggregated statistical data for older persons in the Report.

Malawi has still not conducted the Study recommended by the Commission in the Concluding Observations of the State Report of 2015, aimed at establishing the existence of Indigenous Populations in the country.

The Commission is concerned that the Delegation did not respond to the Commission’s inquiries about the Kayelekera uranium mine which was temporarily closed in 2014 and remains so for the foreseeable future. Information about legislative measures taken by the State to ensure the smooth transition of affected communities from economic dependence on the operations of the Kayelekera mine remains pending.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission makes the following recommendations to Malawi:

Malawi should: i. Continue the regular submission of Periodic Reports on the implementation of the African Charter in compliance with Article 62 of the African Charter; ii. Provide, in its next Periodic Report, up-to-date statistics and data on all relevant sectors as well as on activities of institutions with a human rights mandate; and iii. Inform the Commission, in its next Periodic Report, of the measures taken to address the issues of concern and to ensure the effective implementation of the recommendations contained in these Concluding Observations relating to the African Charter.

Efforts should be made by Malawi to ratify the following Instruments: i. The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Older Persons in Africa; ii. The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa; iii. Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aiming at the abolition of the Death Penalty; iv. Protocol to the OAU Convention on Prevention and Combating of Terrorism; v. Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights; vi. International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families; vii. The Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture; viii. The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; ix. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; x. Optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and xi. Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure.

Malawi should include in its next report, information regarding adequate awareness of the population about their rights, legal procedures and available remedies in respect of their civil and political rights.

Malawi should in its next review period: i. Enact laws to define and expressly criminalize torture in accordance with the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and the Commission’s Robben Island Guidelines; ii. Initiate programs for training law enforcement agents on the Robben Island Guidelines; iii. Ensure that victims of torture and other ill-treatment, including persons with Albinism have the right to all forms of redress including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-repetition in accordance with General Comment No. 4 on the African Charter on Human and People Rights; and iv. Adequately resource the IPCC to enable it discharge its mandate effectively.

Malawi should: i. Improve prison conditions to house more inmates; ii. Create programs and respective spaces for the rehabilitation, education and recreation of prisoners; iii. Provide information on existing sanitary facilities in prisons, as well as information on the distribution of antiretroviral drugs to inmates with HIV-AIDS; iv. Take necessary measures to record and publicize deaths that occur in prisons and places of detention; v. Include matters relating to the protection of human rights in training of law enforcement officials; and vi. Provide Lack information on the number of female Officers recruited in the Police and in the Penitentiary/Correctional Services.

Malawi should: i. Adopt an official moratorium on the death penalty as a positive step towards the definitive abolition of the death penalty; and ii. Provide in its next report, measures taken by State to investigate cases of deaths in prison custody and ensure the trial and punishment of perpetrators where investigation reports suggest unnatural deaths.
Malawi should adopt a Refugee Policy and the Government should ensure that the National Migration Policy is approved by Cabinet.

Malawi should extend opportunities and benefits provided by the post Cyclone Idai Emergency Recovery and Resilience Project to all districts in the region, and ensure that redress to victims of the cyclone is all-inclusive.

Malawi should: i. Enact the draft Bill for older Persons, as well as the 2012 Disability Act which is still under review into law; and ii. Include disaggregated statistical data for older persons in its next periodic Report.

Malawi should provide information in its next periodic Report on the legislative and other measures taken by the State to compensate communities affected by the closure of the Kayelekera uranium mine.

Malawi should undertake the Study referred to in Paragraph 43 of the Initial and Combined Report under reference to ascertain the existence of indigenous populations and communities in the country as recommended by the Commission.
Regarding the implementation of the Maputo Protocol, the Commission notes the following positive aspects:
The Commission notes that there are many positive aspects regarding Malawi’s compliance with its obligations under the Maputo Protocol which it ratified on 20 May 2005.

The Commission commends Malawi for submitting its second Periodic Report in accordance with Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol which is well- articulated and in line with the Guidelines for State Reporting under the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission commends Malawi for the following Laws: i. The Prevention of Domestic Violence Act; ii. The Marriage Divorce and Family Relations Act; iii. The Gender Equality Act and the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; and iv. The Customary Land Act.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Its commitment to the promotion and protection of the rights of women through the enactment of a number of progressive laws aimed at reversing previously discriminatory laws, norms and practices in the country; ii. Adoption and implementation of the Gender Equality Act Implementation and Monitoring Plan for gender equality, integration, influence, empowerment, dignity and opportunities for men and women in Malawi (2016 – 2020); iii. Implementation of Section 11 of the Gender Equality Act which provides that an appointing or recruiting authority in the public service shall appoint no less than forty percent (40%) and no more than sixty percent (60%) of either sex in any department in the public service; iv. Lobbying, advocacy, awareness and sensitization campaigns to reduce gender disparities; v. The Mandatory reporting of Ministries; Departments and Agencies (MDAs) on gender indicators and outcomes of number of women recruited and sent for further studies and trainings through the Organizational Performance Appraisal which MDAs signed with the Office of the President and Cabinet; vi. The public service Sexual Harassment Policy developed to make public service institutions favorable for all gender groups; and vii. Ensuring gender equality and the empowerment of women in the county through several strategies.

The Commission commends Malawi for: i. Male engagement strategy which identifies and prioritizes interventions for involving men and boys in Gender Based Violence (GBV), Sexual Reproductive Health Rights (SRHR) and HIV-related issues; ii. Measures taken to address GBV, including the setup of one stop centres in hospitals; victim support units at Police stations; community support units and the provision of toll free lines; and iii. The establishment of counselling and rehabilitation centres to redress victims of GBV.

The Commission notes with satisfaction: i. The express prohibition of harmful practices as provided for under the HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; ii. Initiatives to combat harmful traditional practices, including activities which clarify toxic cultural and social norms; iv. The 2018 Strategy to end child marriages which is providing guidance in the implementation of interventions targeting girls especially those in rural areas; v. Engagement and lobbying with community leaders including chiefs and religious leaders to become champions for ending child marriages and promoting girls’ education; vi. The minimum age of marriage at 18 under the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act; and the amendment of the Constitution to increase the age of a child as well as the age of consent to marry to 18; vii. The express view by the Malawi Law Commission that Marriage below the age of 18 is a health hazard and that early marriage has negative development implications; and viii. The National Strategy which aims at eradicating child marriage by 2022.

The Commission notes: i. Section 24 (1) (b) (i) of the Constitution which recognises that women can own property separately or jointly and that they are entitled to a fair distribution of the marital property upon dissolution of marriage; and ii. Section 74 of the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act which further provides for equitable distribution of matrimonial property.
The Commission commends Malawi for electoral reforms to include gender quotas in the election of Members of Parliament.

The Commission notes with satisfaction: i. Efforts made by the Government to encourage girl children to stay in school remain and continue with their education such the National Strategy on Inclusive Education 2016 to 2020 with initiatives inter alia: inclusive education projects and Keeping Girls in School; and ii. The Re-Admission Policy in 2016 which provides for the readmission of girls back into school after pregnancy during the COVID-19 Lockdown. The policy also enables pregnant girls to sit for exams during their pregnancy.

The Commission notes with satisfaction, the: i. Domestication of the Maputo Protocol through the enactment of various legislations, including the Gender Equality Act, Marriage Divorce and Family Relations Act and HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Management) Act; ii. Improved status of child mortality and maternal mortality; iii. Measures taken to ensure postnatal care for women including outreach mobile clinics in hard-to-reach areas; information, education and counselling conducted to the communities and antenatal mothers on importance of postnatal care; availability of revised postnatal registers and reporting tools to track performance; and revision of postnatal care guidelines which requires women to be in hospital 48 hours before discharge; and iv. Revision of Post Abortion Care (PAC) Guidelines and community awareness programs on the Guidelines.

The Commission applauds Malawi for: i. The adoption of a National Policy for Older Persons and efforts to establish a Community Elderly Committee; and ii. Plans to introduce Elderly Friendly Health Services which includes geriatric services in existing outreach clinics.
Lack of awareness of the Maputo Protocol results to slow implementation of the Protocol.
In spite of the Government’s efforts to promote and protect the rights of women, the Commission is concerned about the following:

While the Commission appreciates the detailed responses provided by Malawi to the various questions regarding implementation of the Maputo Protocol, the Commission would appreciate more information on the concerns raised by the Commission hereunder.

The Commission is concerned that: i. There is no indication in the Report about how the Government intends to scale up the sensitisation of the gender-related legal instruments and awareness to the grassroots; ii. Gender quotas for political positions and in the private sector still remain problematic; and iii. I mplementation of affirmative action measures for women in the civil service seems to be hampered by patriarchal cultural values which limit women’s access to leadership opportunities.

The Commission is concerned: i. That while the Report states that the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act has been reviewed, there is no indication that the offence of marital rape has been included, and the amended Bill is yet to be presented to Parliament; ii. About lack of data on the registration and acceptance by the authorities of cases for domestic violence; and iii. Sexual harassment especially for women running for public office.
The Commission is concerned that there is no information about other forms of harmful cultural practices in the Report, including widow’s marriage to brother-in-law as an obligation, FGM etc.
While the Commission applauds the protection accorded on the girl child under the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Act, it is concerned that implementation of the Act remains a challenge.
The Commission is concerned by the high illiteracy rate among females and stigma towards pregnant girls on their return to schools.
The Commission is also concerned about the high drop-out rate among girls due to lack of toilets in schools for girls to manage their sanitation needs, especially during their periods.

The Commission is concerned that the Report does not provide any information on the Termination of Pregnancy Bill developed by the Law Commission and yet to be deliberated on and approved by Cabinet at the time of presentation of this Report, even though there have been attempts to take the Bill in Parliament as a Private Members Bill.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission makes the following recommendations to Malawi:
The Government should continue to comply with its obligations under Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol, including by implementing the Commission’s recommendations.

The Government should create more awareness on policies and laws in the country that relate to gender parity and ensure that the awareness campaigns are done across the country, including in the rural areas.

The Government should increase its efforts in challenging deeply rooted beliefs and attitudes surrounding women’s appointment in public and political positions, and implement affirmative actions as stipulated in the Gender Parity Equality Act.
The Government should inform the Commission during its next review, about the status of the amended Prevention of Domestic Violence Act.
The Government should create conditions so that, in practice, sexual harassment that inhibits women from running for public office is reduced.
The Government should take steps to pass a law against sexual harassment.

In its next Periodic Report, the Commission would appreciate more information on other forms of harmful cultural practices that exist in Malawi, including the issue of widows being compelled to marry their brothers-in-law.

The Government should use practical and effective legal, policy and programmatic measures to stop early, child and forced marriage. This should include enforcement of criminal liability for perpetrators, addressing poverty and education causes as well as provision of information on reproductive health to avoid early sexual activity and ultimately early marriages.
The Government should include information on the registration and admissibility by the judiciary bodies of cases brought in the context of marital rape.

The Government should take measures to clearly and firmly lower the illiteracy rate among women and girls, and allow girls to remain in schools, including the creation of specific toilets for them in schools.
The Government should provide in its next Periodic Report, information on the status of the Termination of Pregnancy Bill and reasons for delay in its finalization and enactment into law.

The Commission urges Malawi to also provide in its next Periodic Report, detailed information on the effective implementation of the recommendations made in these Concluding Observations relating to the Maputo Protocol. The Commission requests the Government of Malawi to submit its next periodic report within two years from the notification date of the present Concluding Observations. Adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights at the 70 Ordinary Session held from 23 February to 9 March 2022

The Republic of Cameroon is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter) having ratified it on 20 November 1989. It presented its Combined Periodic Reports (4, 5 and 6) under Article 62 of the African Charter and Initial Reports under Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol and Article 14 of the Kampala Convention during the 67 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission), held virtually in November/December 2020.

The Delegation of the Republic of Cameroon (the Delegation) was led by His Excellency Felix MBAYU, Minister Delegate to the Minister of External Relations in charge of Relations with the Commonwealth.

The Report underscores progress made by Cameroon in the area of human and peoples’ rights as well as legislative, administrative and other measures taken to implement provisions of the African Charter, since the presentation of its 3 Periodic Report at the 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia.

The Commission notes with satisfaction the inclusive and participatory approach in the preparation of the Report, in particular, the establishment of an inter-ministerial committee responsible for drafting reports and monitoring the implementation of human rights-related recommendations, with the involvement of the National Human Rights Commission, other institutions of the Republic and representatives of human rights organizations.
It commends the Republic of Cameroon for its Report which includes detailed statistics and relevant analyses of the current human rights situation as well as challenges.

It welcomes measures taken to implement recommendations made by the Commission following the consideration of Cameroon’s 3 Periodic Report at the 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia.

The Commission commends the Delegation of Cameroon for the open and constructive dialogue which prevailed during the presentation of the Periodic Reports and for the quality of the information provided in response to the concerns raised by the members of the Commission.

These Concluding Observations are divided into three parts: a first part on the African Charter followed by recommendations, a second part which focuses on the Maputo Protocol and is also followed by recommendations, and finally a third part on the Kampala Convention with recommendations. Part A: African Charter On Human and Peoples’ Rights - Article 62:

The Commission takes note of the presentation by the Republic of Cameroon of its 4, 5 and 6 Periodic Reports on the implementation of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights during the 67 Ordinary Session held virtually in November/December 2020.

It welcomes the commitment of Cameroon, which is now up to date with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter. Recommendation: - The Republic of Cameroon should include a separate and detailed section in its next Report describing actions taken to implement the recommendations made by the Commission. - Ratifications

The Commission takes good note of the ratification by Cameroon, during the reporting period, of several human rights instruments, both at the level of the African Union and the UN, as well as other sub-regional conventions and bilateral agreements aimed at improving the rights of Cameroonians. : - Ensure that the ratification process of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities is completed and take the necessary steps to ratify the following instruments: o Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa; o Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Citizens to Social Protection and Social Security; o The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; and - Make the Declaration under Article 36(4) of the Protocol on the establishment of the African Court to allow full access to justice for all Cameroonians. Article 1: Legislative measures to incorporate the provisions of the African Charter into domestic laws

The Commission welcomes the adoption, by the Government of the Republic of Cameroon, of several legislative texts relating to human rights promotion and protection since the presentation of its last Report. Recommendation: The Republic of Cameroon should pursue efforts aimed at incorporating the provisions of international human rights instruments into its domestic laws, notably by finalizing the adoption of the laws on associations, trafficking in persons and human rights defenders. It should also ensure the effective implementation of adopted laws by conducting outcome assessments. Article 25: Duty to promote human rights NHRIs and other institutions

The Commission commends Cameroon on the establishment of the Human Rights Commission of Cameroon (2019) to replace the National Commission on Human Rights and Freedoms. Recommendation: - The Republic of Cameroon should ensure that the Human Rights Commission has the necessary financial and human resources to carry out its full mandate as a National Human Rights Institution. Article 2: Right to freedom from discrimination
The Commission takes note of the provisions included in the Criminal Code punishing acts of discrimination.

However, it is concerned about the lack of information on measures taken to educate the population in this respect. Recommendation: - Ensure that awareness-raising campaigns are carried out on the issue of discrimination and that discriminatory acts are effectively punished as provided by law. Article 3: Right to equality before the law and to the equal protection of the law

The Commission notes Cameroon’s efforts to ensure equality before the law for all. Nevertheless, it is concerned about the difficulties faced by some litigants and lawyers before the courts as a result of the lack of adequate measures to take the English language into consideration.

The Commission is also concerned about the continued prosecution of civilians in military courts. Recommendations: - Ensure that measures are taken for all litigants to bring cases before the courts in their preferred language (English or French); and - Ensure that civilians are tried in civil courts for better administration of justice. Article 4: Right to life
The Commission is concerned that the death penalty is still maintained in the law, even as a deterrent, as the possibility is there to use it at any time.

Furthermore, although the State has indicated that it is improving the living conditions of all prisoners, no details on these improvements have been given. - The Republic of Cameroon should take the necessary measures to abolish the death penalty; and - Provide information on the measures taken to improve the living conditions of prisoners, particularly those on death row. Article 5: Prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment

The Commission takes note that the mandate of the CDHC was extended to include the prerogatives of the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture in respect of the State’s obligations under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (OPCAT). Article 6: Right to personal liberty and protection against arbitrary detention
The Commission notes the establishment of a Commission for the compensation of victims of police custody and abusive pre-trial detention.

Yet, the duration of pre-trial detention is still an issue. Recommendation: - Address the recurrent issue of prolonged pre-trial detention by implementing the Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-trial Detention in Africa. Article 7: Right to a fair trial

The Commission notes with satisfaction the changes in the organisation of the Supreme Court pursuant to Law No. 2017/014 of 12 July 2017, which established a Common Law Division under the Judicial Chamber to improve access to justice for litigants with a common law background, as well as the appointment of members of Legal Aid Commissions to the judicial courts.

It also notes that the functioning of legal aid commissions was hampered by financial constraints, which therefore limited its full enjoyment by litigants. - Ensure that the new organisational structure of the Supreme Court is widely disseminated to the public and that adequate support measures are put in place (translators and interpreters); and - Increase the budget for legal aid. Article 9: Right to receive information and freedom of speech

The Commission takes due note of the information contained in the Report on the measures taken to maintain media diversity and to address the challenges of electronic media, including social networks.
The Commission also notes the organisation of various training courses for journalists and media professionals.

However, the Commission notes the need to protect access to the internet for all citizens without restriction, while recognising the importance of regulation. Recommendations: - Ensure the full implementation of safeguards relating to access to information, notably those included in Law No. 2015/007 of 20 April 2015 governing audiovisual activity in Cameroon; - Develop an Information, Communication and Digital Information Act; and - Adhere to the 2019 Declaration on Freedom of Expression. Articles 10 and 11: Right to freedom of association and assembly

The Commission is concerned about the lack of a specific legal framework for the protection of human rights defenders and the multiple reports of arbitrary arrests and other acts of harassment of individuals working to promote and protect human rights, particularly in the context of the socio-political crisis in the northern and eastern regions of Cameroon. - Adopt a specific law on human rights defenders; - Ensure a safe working environment for human rights defenders; - Ensure that the implementation of the law on associations is in line with the Guidelines on Freedom of Association and Assembly of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights; and - Guarantee the right to peaceful assembly without space and time restrictions that render this right meaningless. Article 12: Right to freedom of movement

The Commission notes the various measures taken by the State in terms of support to refugees and asylum seekers as well as the positive cooperation with UNHCR in this respect. Recommendation: - Continue efforts to mainstream local integration as a solution for long-term refugees and not only in the context of a cessation clause; local integration can reduce conventional refugee support costs. Article 13: Right to participate in government
The information contained in the Report demonstrates the will of the Republic of Cameroon to ensure the participation of all population subsets in the management of public affairs.

However, the Commission notes that the figures given for voter registration do not refer to the number of men, thus making it difficult to determine whether gender parity is effectively respected or progress has been made in that respect. - Continue efforts to include all categories while ensuring that quotas are set for this purpose to ensure greater equity; and - Provide figures on the number of women, young people, people with disabilities and indigenous minorities in decision-making positions. Article 14: Right to property/ right to housing Right to property

The Commission takes note of the measures adopted to secure access to land, the regulatory framework to protect the needs of vulnerable groups as reflected in the fight against land grabbing and consultations with customary and indigenous communities, measures to protect against violations of land rights, judicial protection of the right to property and the conditions for compensation in the event of expropriation in the public interest. It also takes note of the establishment of an ad hoc committee in charge of reviewing the proposals of Cameroon’s traditional leaders on the ongoing land, forestry and mining reform.
The Commission hopes that the reform will strengthen existing safeguards and protection of the right to property for all in Cameroon. Right to housing
