Le Comité note que les victimes qui étaient des enfants au moment où les violations alléguées ont eu lieu sont maintenant tous des adultes âgées entre 22 ans et 35 ans au moment où les plaignants saisissaient le Comité. En outre, aucune mesure n’a été prise par les plaignants ou les victimes en tant que adultes, pour régler la question du moment où les violations alléguées se sont produites jusqu’au jour où le Comité a été saisie.

En tenant compte de la complexité de l’affaire en l’espèce, le Comité estime qu’il convient d’établir une distinction entre l’exigence de la soumission de la Communication dans un délai raisonnable après l’épuisement des voies de recours internes comme condition de recevabilité tel qu’il ressort du libellé de la Section IX (1) (E) et le retard apparent dans la présentation de la Communication. En effet, la condition de la soumission de la Communication dans un délai raisonnable après l’épuisement des voies de recours internes ne fait pas l’objet de la présente analyse étant donné que les parties ne soulèvent aucune exception quant à cette condition de recevabilité et en tenant compte que le contrôle de condition de délai raisonnable est conditionné, sauf exception, par rapport à l’épuisement des recours internes pertinents. S’agissant du retard apparent dans la soumission de la communication, le Comité considère que le comportement de victimes et des plaignants dans la poursuite de leurs cas est déterminant dans la présente Communication. Bien qu'il n'y ait pas de délai prévu par les Directives révisées sur les Communications sur le nombre d'années au cours desquelles les affaires doivent être soumises au Comité , le Comité s'inspire de l'approche du Comité des Droits de l'Homme dans l’affaire Gobin c. Maurice selon laquelle le Comité a conclu que faute d'explication, la présentation de la Communication après un délai aussi long doit être considérée comme un abus du droit de plainte. Par conséquent, aucun retard n'est acceptable sans justification raisonnable et qu’il incombe sur les plaignants qui allèguent des violations, agissent avec la diligence requise dans la poursuite de leurs cas. Le Comité constate que le retard dans la présentation de la Communication n'est pas étayées par des justifications raisonnable ou de preuves tangibles.

En outre, pour ce qui est de l’allégation selon laquelle les recours sont inefficaces, le Comité en reprend le raisonnement de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l’Homme et des Peuples dans l’affaire Anuak Justice Council c. Ethiopie a conclu dans sa Décision sur la Communication Minority Rights Group International and SOS- Esclaves au nom de Sid Ould Salem and Yarg Ould Salem contre le gouvernement de la République Islamique de Mauritanie qu’un recours est efficace s'il offre une perspective de réussite. Si son succès n'est pas suffisamment certain, le recours ne peut pas répondre aux exigences de disponibilité et d'efficacité. De plus, un recours est considéré comme suffisant s'il est en mesure de redresser la plainte. Le Comité relève qu’il ressort du dossier, que l’État défendeur a fourni des copies des jugements rendus par les juridictions internes. Le Comité note que ces recours ont abouti à remédier aux griefs des enfants victimes de mariage forcé et par conséquent conclu l’existence des recours internes à épuiser par les victimes et les plaignants de la présente Communication avant de la saisir. Le Comité note cependant, que les 12 CDH, Communication 767/1997, M. Vishwadeo Gobin c. Maurice,Décidée lors de la 72e session, 16 juillet 2001, CCPR/C/72/D/787/1997, para 6.3. 13 CAEDBE, Legal and Human Rights Center and Center for Reproductive Rights c. République-Unie de Tanzanie, para29, ACHPR, Communications 147/95 and 149/96, Sir Dawda K Jawara v The Gambia, (May 2000), para 31 14 CAEDBE, Communication no 007/com/003/2015, Minority Rights Group International and SOS-Esclaves au nom de Sid Ould Salem et Yarg Ould Salem c. le Gouvernement de la République de Mauritanie, Para 23. arguments des Plaignants qui portent surtout sur l’inefficacité de ces voies de recours internes et leur capacité à remédier aux violations alléguées, sont sans fondement et ne sont pas étayées par des preuves.

En tout état de cause, s’agissant de la preuve de l’épuisement des recours internes, le Comité considère qu’il incombait aux victimes et à leurs représentants de veiller à disposer de tous les faits et arguments pertinents aux fins de prouver l’épuisement des recours internes. L’épuisement des voies de recours internes est une exigence du droit international et non une question de choix. Le fait qu’ils n’aient pas essayé d’épuiser les voies de recours internes avant de le saisir, mais seulement des années après que les faits allégués se soient produits, n’exonère pas les demandeurs de l’obligation d’épuiser les recours internes disponibles.

Selon la Cour Africaine des Droits de l’Homme et des Peuples dans l’affaire Diakité c. Mali, la preuve de l’épuisement des voies de recours internes repose sur les demandeurs qui doivent apporter la preuve d’avoir entrepris toutes les démarches nécessaires pour épuiser ou essayer d’épuiser toutes les voies de recours internes mises à leur disposition et il ne suffit pas que le plaignant mette en doute l’efficacité des recours internes de l’État du fait d’incidences isolées. De surcroît, les plaignants doivent joindre tous les éléments de preuve pertinents attestant les mesures prises pour épuiser les voies de recours internes voire même la preuve d’une tentative d’épuisement des recours internes.

Selon la Cour Européenne de Droits de l’Homme dans l’affaire SCOPPOLA c. Italie les « principes de droit international généralement reconnus », certaines circonstances particulières peuvent dispenser le requérant de l'obligation d'épuiser les voies de recours internes qui s'offrent à lui. Toutefois, le simple fait de nourrir des doutes quant aux perspectives de succès d'un recours donné, qui n'est pas de toute évidence voué à l'échec, ne constitue pas une raison valable pour justifier la non- utilisation de recours internes.

Le même raisonnement a été adopté par la Cour Africaine des Droits de l’Homme et des Peuples dans l’affaire Mango et autres c. Tanzanie, dans laquelle elle a conclu que « [l]es requérants auraient pu saisir la Haute Cour […] et qu’ils n’auraient pas dû ignorer de manière désinvolte (sic) les recours disponibles de l’État défendeur sans même tenter de les exercer ».

Le Comité note que la présente Communication ne contient aucune information sur les actions prises devant les juridictions internes par les plaignants en vue de mettre fin aux violations alléguées. Pour autant, le Comité en constatant qu’il est important d’insister sur le fait qu’aucune des dix victimes ou de leurs représentants n’a soulevé 15 CAEDBE, Communication No. 010/Com/003/2016, Mr. and Mrs. Elogo Menye and Rev. Daniel Ezo’o Ayo Represeted by Etoungou Nko’o Law Firm c. République du Cameroun, para 24. 16 CourADHP,Affaire Peter Joseph Chacha c. Tanzanie no 003/2012, 28 mars 2014,para 142. 17 CourADHP,Diakité c. Mali, no 009/2016, 28 septembre 2017, (2017) 2 RJCA 122, para. 53. 18 Voir Anuak Justice Council c. Ethiopie Communication no. 299/2005, para 48. 19 CEDH, Affaire SCOPPOLA c. ITALIE (No 2) (Requête no 10249/03) Arret 2009 para 70. une seule action qui lui soit propre avant de le saisir, conclu que les plaignants anticipaient l'inefficacité du recours local en émettant simplement des doutes sans essayer d'épuiser un quelconque recours au niveau local. Par conséquent, le Comité conclut que la présente Communication ne remplit pas la condition de recevabilité énoncée dans la Section IX (1) (D).

Sur la base des arguments et de l'analyse ci-dessus, le Comité Africain d'Experts sur les Droits et le Bien-être de l'Enfant note et conclut que la Communication soumise par l'auteur ne remplit pas les conditions de recevabilité ; les plaignants n’ayant pas épuisé les voies de recours locales.
La Communication est donc déclarée irrecevable. Adoptée lors de la 39ème session ordinaire du CAEDBE tenue virtuellement du 21 Mars au 01 Avril 2022.

The Secretariat of the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Committee / ACERWC) received a Communication dated 8 December 2021 pursuant to Article 44(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Charter / ACRWC). The Communication was submitted by the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and the Association pour la Promotion du Développement Local (APDL) (on behalf of Fadimatou Mohamadou and 9 others) (the Complainants) against the Republic of Cameroon.
Pursuant to Section III of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications, the Secretariat carried out a preliminary review and registered it under No. 0018/Com/002/2021.

Pursuant to Section IX(2)(iv) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications by the ACERWC (the Revised Guidelines on Communications), the Committee transmitted a copy of the Communication to the Respondent State Party by Note Verbale (Ref: ACE/OL/10/309.21) dated 21 December 2021 and invited it to submit arguments on the admissibility of the Communication within 60 days from the date of receipt of the Secretariat’s request. The Secretariat received the State Party’s response to the Communication on 23 February 2022. Pursuant to Section IX(2)(vi) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications by the ACERWC (the Revised Guidelines on Communications), the Secretariat transmitted the Respondent State’s response to the Complainants by letter (Ref: ACE/OL/10/089.22) dated 2 March 2022 so that they could submit their observations on the State Party’s response within 30 days of receipt of the State Party’s observations. Consequently, the Secretariat received the Complainants’ observations on 17 March 2022.

In their Communication filed with the Committee, the Complainants report that Fadimatou Mohamadou and 9 others, aged between 22 and 35 years, were married when they were still minors aged between 13 and 17 years.

The Complainants argue that civil legislation on marriage in Cameroon maintains provisions that enshrine child marriage. Moreover, they argue that criminal legislation in Cameroon also fails to offer effective protection to victims of child marriage. According to the Complainants, the Cameroonian Penal Code, in particular the provisions of Article 356, paragraph 3, criminalises the marriage of minors, but minor victims cannot avail themselves of that protection because Article 71, paragraph 1 of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure requires that children be represented by their parents.

The Communication further alleges that, by maintaining the provisions of the Civil Code authorising early marriages in Article 144 of the Cameroonian Civil Code, the State Party failed in its duty to adopt the legislative measures necessary to protect Cameroonian girls against child marriage. The Complainants allege that the Respondent State violated the following rights provided for in the international instruments to which it is a party: i. Articles 1(1) and (3) and 21(2) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child on the obligation to adopt legislative measures protecting Cameroonian girls against child marriage; ii. Articles 3 and 21.1.b of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and Article 2 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol) on combating discrimination against women and girls; ii. Article 4.1 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child on the best interests of the child; iii. Articles 11.1 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and Article 12.2.c) of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol) on the right to education.
The Complainants argue that the Communication meets the admissibility requirement under Section XI(1) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications.

The Complainants focus in particular on the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies and argue that there is an exception to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies, as they contended that girls who are victims of child marriage have practically no judicial remedies in Cameroon.

The Complainants allege that, despite Article 25 of the Cameroonian Constitution, individuals (including victims) cannot challenge the provisions of the Civil Code that authorise child marriage in order to change or amend them, because in Cameroon the initiative of laws belongs solely and/or concurrently to the President of the Republic and the members of Parliament.

The Complainants allege that even though the Cameroonian Penal Code criminalises the marriage of minors in Article 356, paragraph 3, minor victims cannot set the public prosecution in motion. The reason is that, under Article 71, paragraph 1 of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure, minor victims must be represented by their parents and, consequently and logically, the parents cannot seize the competent judicial authorities, whether by complaint or by report, since it is they themselves who force the girls into early marriage. They cannot thus complain about or report facts of which they are the perpetrators, hence early marriages go unpunished.
The Complainants further observe that in such circumstances local remedies are not available, effective and accessible in cases of child marriage.

The Complainants cite Communication 147/95 & 149/96: Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. Gambia, in which the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights held that remedies are available, effective and accessible when they can be used without obstacles.

Following the reference to Communication No. 006/Com/002/2015 – Institute for Human Right and Development in Africa and Finders Group Initiative on behalf of TFA (a minor) against the Government the Republic of Cameroon, the Complainants note that the Committee adopted the understanding of an available remedy as defined by the Commission in Communication No. 299/2005 – Anuak Justice Council v. Ethiopia and specified that an available remedy is one that is within the victim’s reach.

The Complainants state that, for victims of child marriage in Cameroon, the remedy existing in Cameroon is not within their reach because they face obstacles of two kinds. First, being minors, they lack the capacity to bring an action and to seize the competent criminal courts (cf. Article 71, paragraph 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). Whereas child marriages constitute offences under Cameroonian positive law, the parents or guardians of the victims should in principle seize the Police or the Public Prosecutor’s Office by way of complaint or report, but in practice they cannot report themselves because they are perpetrators or accomplices.

The Complainants state that it remains for the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Judicial Police to carry out their work of prosecution in cases of child marriage, which they are not currently doing.

Finally, the Complainants argue that, because judicial avenues are practically closed to victims of child marriage, local remedies are practically not available, effective and accessible to girls who are minors and victims of early marriage in Cameroon, which constitutes an exception to the exhaustion of local remedies as a condition of admissibility of the present Communication.

The Respondent State, in its statement of defence, submits that the Communication is inadmissible because it does not meet the requirements set out in the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications. The Respondent State raises in particular the objection of inadmissibility on the ground that the Communication is unfounded and that the Complainants have not exhausted local remedies.

The first point raised concerns what the Government called the unfounded nature of the Communication. The Respondent State argues that the authors of the Communication produced handwritten documents entitled “declaration and authorisation of representation”, which were allegedly drafted and signed by the person named FADIMATOU MAHOMADOU and 9 others, who allegedly affixed their fingerprints to them.

The Respondent State argues that a brief look at those documents shows, in form and substance, that they were drafted by one and the same person. It is alleged that the said girls were deprived of their right to education, yet these documents were drafted by a person with a good knowledge of the French language; all of which leads to the conclusion that these documents do not in any way originate from the said girls.
The Respondent State further argues that the facts of child marriage alleged therein are not supported by any evidence, whether testimonial or documentary.

With regard to the inadmissibility based on non-exhaustion of local remedies, the Respondent State argues that the Communication should be declared inadmissible because the Complainants did not exhaust local remedies, in that they never raised the grievances now before the Committee before any of its courts of first instance, and did not see fit to pursue local remedies; all of which would nevertheless have enabled the Republic of Cameroon, had the alleged facts of child marriage been established, to provide an appropriate response.

In its observations on the statement of defence, the Respondent State argues that the applicants did not exhaust local remedies before seizing the Committee. It contends that, contrary to the Complainants’ statements, local remedies are available and effective for cases of child marriage in Cameroon.

As regards the availability of local remedies, the Respondent State argues that child marriage constitutes the offence of forced marriage within the meaning of Article 356, paragraph 3 of the Cameroonian Penal Code.

The Respondent State, referring to the Committee’s jurisprudence in the case of Children of Nubian Descent, adds that, pursuant to Articles 40 et seq., 135 et seq. and 157 et seq. of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP), victims of offences have several remedies at their disposal, namely the complaint, the direct summons and the complaint with civil-party application. These remedies are available, accessible and can be pursued by everyone without hindrance. More specifically, being exempt from fees and from any age-related condition, the complaint may be addressed either to the Public Prosecutor, or to a Judicial Police Officer (JPO), or to an administrative authority which is required to pass it on to the first-mentioned. These authorities cannot refuse to receive the complaint, which systematically gives rise to the opening of an investigation and to prosecution where sufficient evidence is gathered.

The Respondent State adds that one of the important measures was the adoption of Law No. 2016/007 of 12 July 2016 on the Penal Code, whose Article 356 on forced marriage makes child marriage, without discrimination, a criminal offence. Accordingly, it sets the minimum age of marriage at 18 years for girls and boys alike. That text renders null and void all prior contrary provisions on the age of marriage, notably those contained in the Civil Code and in Ordinance No. 81/002 of 29 June 1981 on the organisation of civil status and various provisions relating to the status of natural persons, as amended and supplemented by Law No. 2011/011 of 6 May 2011

As regards the effectiveness of local remedies, the Respondent State argues that, contrary to the assertions of the authors of the Communication, whether the remedy is pursued by the victim or by the public prosecutor’s office, facts of child marriage give rise to sanctions where proof is adduced. Related offences are also punished. This is generally the case of indecent assault in the presence of a person under 16 years of age or of indecent assault in the presence of a person aged 16 to 21 years (Articles 346 and 346 of the PC).

The Respondent State states that in practice, following a complaint or a report of child marriage, an investigation is opened by a Judicial Police Officer and closed by a record (procès-verbal), which is transmitted to the Public Prosecutor. That magistrate may either decide to close the case without further action in the absence of sufficient evidence and inform the complainant (who may decide to institute proceedings), or order further investigation, or else set the public prosecution in motion, depending on the circumstances, by way of flagrante delicto procedure, direct summons or judicial investigation.

By way of illustration, the Respondent State in its response cited 3 recent judgments delivered respectively in 2016, 2018 and 2020 by the High Court of Benue and the Court of First Instance of Mora which illustrate this criterion. The judgments delivered in the three cases found the accused guilty of the facts with which they were charged, including forced marriage, attempted forced marriage, indecent assault in the presence of a person under 16 years of age followed by sexual intercourse, and abduction of a child and arrest, and imposed heavy sentences on them.
In their observations, the Complainants maintain their arguments on the merits of the present Communication.

The Complainants recall that child marriages have, among many other consequences, a harmful effect on the full enjoyment of the right to education, hence the majority of minors married early cannot draft the representation instruments and the statements of facts in French, a language learned and mastered by those who were not forced to leave school because of early marriage.

The Complainants argue that, since the victims cannot send the Committee documents in their mother tongues, which are not languages used by the Committee, they have no other choice but to have recourse to a third person who voluntarily offers to draft their instruments in French so that they can finally bring the situations of violations of their rights to the attention of the Committee, which is a mechanism that uses French as one of its official languages.

The Complainants emphasise that the survivors represented in the present Communication fully recognise themselves in the instruments drafted by a person in whom they freely placed their trust, recounting to him everything that happened to them in the language that suits them, for transcription into French. They identify themselves as the authors of the content of these documents challenged by the Respondent State and, as proof, they affixed their signature or fingerprints to them and provided their identity documents to further attest that it is the violation of their rights that is being brought to the attention of the Committee.

The Complainants moreover argue that no instrument of the Committee prohibits survivors of violations from having recourse to a person in order to bring their situation to the attention of the Committee, especially in an official language of the African Union that these survivors do not master.

Concerning the Respondent State’s argument that the facts constituting the violations brought before the Committee are not corroborated by evidence, the Complainants argue that the child marriages at issue in this Communication are not recorded in the official registers, which is once again in contradiction with Cameroon’s obligations under the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, since customary and religious marriages must be entered in the civil status registers.
The Complainants add that, in the case of the survivors in the present Communication, the child marriages were celebrated by Imams in mosques but leave no trace in the civil status registers.

The Complainants clearly contested the objection of inadmissibility for non-exhaustion of local remedies raised by the Respondent State and reaffirmed that local remedies are not available and effective.

The Committee notes that the present Communication is submitted in accordance with Article 44 of the ACRWC, which allows the Committee to receive and consider complaints from “any person, group or non-governmental organization recognized by the Organization of African Unity, by a Member State, or by the United Nations relating to any matter covered by [the Charter]”. The Committee also notes that the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and APDEL are duly registered in The Gambia and Cameroon respectively. The Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) is a pan-African non-governmental organisation based in Banjul, The Gambia, and APDEL is an organisation under Cameroonian law with consultative status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council. Furthermore, it is also noted that the Communication is directed against the Republic of Cameroon (hereinafter “the Respondent State”), a State Party to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (hereinafter “the Charter”) since 23 June 1999, and within whose jurisdiction the alleged violations of the rights enshrined in the Charter are said to have been committed.

Taking into account the requirements set out in Section (I) of the Revised Guidelines on Communications, the Complainants meet the requirements for access to the Committee since they are registered in Member States of the African Union; it is also noted that their Communication is filed on behalf of Fadimatou Mohamadou and 9 other women who were still children at the time the alleged violations occurred, in accordance with Section I(4)(a) of the Revised Guidelines on Communications, according to which the Committee’s jurisdiction is determined by the age of the child at the time of the alleged violation.
Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the applicants are entitled to submit a Communication in accordance with Article 44 of the ACRWC.

In analysing the admissibility of the Communication, the Committee assesses whether the admissibility requirements set out in Section IX(1) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications are met.

Section IX(1)(A) of the Revised Guidelines provides that a Communication must be compatible with the provisions of the Constitutive Act of the African Union or with the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. The Complainants argue that this requirement is met since the Communication is submitted in accordance with Article 44 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child in order to strengthen respect for the provisions of the Charter in Cameroon and to contribute to the establishment of a strong and legally coherent African child rights regime. The Committee notes that the Communication is compatible with the Constitutive Act of the AU and the Charter since it concerns violations of the provisions of the Charter. In this regard, the Committee reiterates its Decision in the Talibés case, in which it considered that the requirement of compatibility with the Constitutive Act of the AU and the Charter is met if a Communication alleges violations of the ACRWC. The Committee notes that the present Communication alleges the violation of specific provisions of the Charter and of the Maputo Protocol and is therefore submitted in conformity with the provisions of the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Communication satisfies the requirements of Section (1)(A) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications.
The Committee also notes that the Communication is presented in professional, polite and respectful language, which makes it compatible with Section (1)(F) of the Revised Guidelines.

In accordance with Section IX(1)(B) of the Revised Guidelines, the Communication should not be exclusively based on information disseminated by the media or be manifestly unfounded. In the present case, the Respondent State contested the admissibility of the Communication on the ground that it is unfounded, on the one hand, on the basis that the declaration and authorisation of representation do not originate from the victims, and, on the other hand, on the basis of the absence of evidence, whether testimonial or documentary, of the facts of child marriage alleged therein.

As regards the State Party’s argument on the question of the identity of the victims, the Committee noted that the factual basis of the present Communication derives from the direct testimony of the victims. More specifically, the Committee notes that the applicants are identified as the authors of the content of those documents inasmuch as the attached documents were signed; they affixed their signature or fingerprints to them and provided their identity documents to further attest that it is the violation of their rights that is being brought to the attention of the Committee. With regard to the question of formal evidence of the facts of child marriage alleged therein, the Complainants argue that the child marriages at issue in this Communication are not recorded in the official registers because, in the case of the survivors in the present Communication, the child marriages were celebrated by imams in mosques but leave no trace in the civil status registers. In this regard, the Committee, referring to the definition of child marriage given in the Joint General Comment of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) and the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) on Ending Child Marriage, according to which child marriage is a marriage “any formal marriage or informal union between a man and a woman that is recognised by any system of law, custom, society or religion” in which one or both parties is or was a child under the age of 18 at the time of the union.

In this sense, in such an assessment of the said circumstances and of the particular context surrounding child marriage, the marriage may be formal or informal, governed by civil law or religion, or may simply be a custom. Moreover, it happens that marriages are recognised by the community without any legal registration. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Communication satisfies the requirement of Section IX(1)(B).

In accordance with Section IX(1)(C) of the Revised Guidelines on Communications, in accordance with the legal instruments of the African Union and the principles of the Charter of the United Nations. As regards the Committee’s examination, the Communication under consideration does not raise matters pending or previously settled by another international body or procedure in accordance with the legal instruments of the African Union and the principles of the Charter of the United Nations. The Committee therefore considers that the Communication has satisfied the requirement of Section IX(1)(C) of the Revised Guidelines.

Section IX(1)(D) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications provides that the author of a Communication must have exhausted all available and accessible local remedies before bringing the matter before the Committee. Although the Complainants argue that local remedies are not available, effective and accessible in cases of child marriage in Cameroon, whereas the Respondent State argues that local remedies are indeed available and effective, the Committee considers that the question of the exhaustion of local remedies requires a detailed explanation. A priori, it would be obvious to say that the rule of exhaustion of local remedies is a procedural rule of customary international law according to which, prior to seizing an international court of a given case, the applicant is under an obligation to raise that case, at least in substance, before the national authorities. It follows that the ratio legis of requiring such an obligation is to reinforce the subsidiary and complementary relationship of the international system to the national system. In principle, a body such as the ACERWC should not take the place of a Court of First Instance. It should intervene only as a last resort, after local remedies have been exhausted and have failed.

As the Committee noted in its previous Decisions, one of the main objectives of the exhaustion of local remedies, which is also linked to the notion of State sovereignty, is to enable the Respondent State to be the first port of call for dealing with alleged violations at the national level. This principle was affirmed by the Committee as early as the Children of Nubian Descent case. In the same vein, the Committee also invoked this principle in its Decision on admissibility in the case of Legal and Human Rights Center and Center for Reproductive Rights v. United Republic of Tanzania, in full harmony with the jurisprudence of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, where it stated that “the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies is not to create an obstacle to access to remedies at the supranational level, but rather to ensure that States are given the information on the alleged violations and an opportunity to redress those violations within the limits of their available means. States must be informed in detail of these violations occurring before being called before an international or regional court. 2 AfCHPR, Case of Sébastien Germain Ajavon v. Benin, No. 013/2017, 29 March 2019, para. 98. 3 ACERWC, Communication No. 010/Com/003/2016, Mr. and Mrs. Elogo Menye and Rev. Daniel Ezo’o Ayo Represeted by Etoungou Nko’o Law Firm v. Republic of Cameroon, para 23. 4 ACERWC, Communication No. Com/002/2009, Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and the Open Society Justice Initiative (on behalf of Children of Nubian descent in Kenya); para. 33. 5 ACERWC, Communication No: 0012/Com/001/2019, Legal and Human Rights Center and Center for Reproductive Rights v. United Republic of Tanzania, para 26.

In the present case, as regards the existence of exceptions to the rule of exhaustion of remedies, raised by the Complainants, the Committee recalls at the outset that this exhaustion requirement may be waived exceptionally where local remedies are not available, are ineffective or insufficient, or where the proceedings before domestic courts are unduly prolonged.

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights has stressed that “Where a complainant argues that a particular remedy need not be exhausted because it is unavailable, ineffective or insufficient, the procedure is as follows: 1. The complainant states that the remedy need not be exhausted because it is ineffective (unavailable or insufficient), which remains to be proved; 2. The Respondent State must then demonstrate that the remedy is available, effective and sufficient; and 3. If the Respondent State is able to establish this, then the complainant must demonstrate that he or she has actually exhausted the remedy or that the remedy was not effective with regard to this specific case, even if it may be effective in general”. Moreover, the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies requires that the State be given, in the first place, the opportunity to resolve the question of the violation.

As clarified by the Committee in its previous Decisions, the rule of exhaustion of local remedies requires that only available, effective and adequate (sufficient) local remedies must be exhausted. In applying this rule, if the Complainants manage to demonstrate the absence of one of these criteria, this means that they are no longer under the obligation to exhaust local remedies. Conversely, the author of a Communication must exhaust all available and accessible local remedies before seizing the Committee, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged or ineffective. It follows that, where a complainant argues that a particular remedy need not be exhausted because it is unavailable, ineffective or insufficient, the complainant must be able to demonstrate that the remedies will not satisfy these criteria in practice, and not simply in the opinion of the victim or of his or her legal representative.

The Committee takes note of the Complainants’ argument that they cannot seek the exhaustion of local remedies because of their inability to challenge the provisions of the Civil Code that authorise child marriage in order to change or amend them, since in Cameroon, according to Article 25 of the Constitution, the initiative of laws belongs solely and/or concurrently to the President of the Republic and the members of Parliament. In this regard, the Committee, referring to its jurisprudence in the Children of Nubian Descent case, recalls what is envisaged in the Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications, and also supported by the jurisprudence of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, that for a Communication to be admissible before it, extraordinary remedies of a non-judicial nature do not fall within the notion of “local remedies” which the complainants must have exhausted, and stresses that a complainant is required to exhaust only the ordinary judicial remedies before seizing it.

The Complainants further observe that, for victims of child marriage in Cameroon, the existing remedy is not within their reach because they face obstacles of two kinds. On the one hand, being minors, they lack the capacity to bring an action and to seize the competent criminal courts. Whereas child marriages constitute offences under Cameroonian positive law, the parents or guardians of the victims should in principle seize the Police or the Public Prosecutor’s Office by way of complaint or report, but in practice they cannot report themselves because they are the perpetrators or accomplices; and, on the other hand, it remains for the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Judicial Police to carry out their work of prosecution in cases of child marriage, which they are not currently doing.

In its statement of defence, the Respondent State states that child marriage constitutes the offence of forced marriage within the meaning of Article 356, paragraph 3 of the Cameroonian Penal Code and that victims of offences have several remedies at their disposal, namely the complaint, the direct summons and the complaint with civil-party application.

As regards the arguments of both parties on the availability of local remedies, the Committee recalls that the availability of a local remedy is assessed according to the complainants’ ability to use the remedy in their case. The Committee notes that, in the present case, child marriage constitutes an offence within the meaning of Article 356, paragraph 3 of the Cameroonian Penal Code. However, while taking into account the Complainants’ argument that children in Cameroon are not able to exercise this right given the obstacles they face, as appears from the provisions of Article 71, paragraph 1 of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure, under which a child has no right to initiate judicial proceedings before the courts in his or her own name and, consequently, any legal action seeking to challenge violations of a child’s rights must be brought by his or her legal representative, the Committee is of the view that the crucial question arising in determining the admissibility of the present Communication is the excessive delay recorded in seizing the Committee. The Committee notes that the victims, who were children at the time the alleged violations took place, were all adults aged between 22 and 35 years at the time the Complainants seized the Committee. Furthermore, no measure was taken by the Complainants or by the victims as adults to address the matter from the time the alleged violations occurred until the day the Committee was seized.

Taking into account the complexity of the present case, the Committee considers that a distinction should be drawn between the requirement that the Communication be submitted within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of local remedies as a condition of admissibility, as appears from the wording of Section IX(1)(E), and the apparent delay in submitting the Communication. Indeed, the requirement of submitting the Communication within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of local remedies is not the subject of the present analysis, given that the parties raise no objection regarding this admissibility requirement and taking into account that the review of the reasonable time requirement is, save for exceptions, conditional upon the exhaustion of the relevant local remedies. As regards the apparent delay in submitting the communication, the Committee considers that the conduct of the victims and of the Complainants in pursuing their cases is decisive in the present Communication. Although the Revised Guidelines on Communications provide no time limit as to the number of years within which cases must be submitted to the Committee, the Committee draws inspiration from the approach of the Human Rights Committee in the case of Gobin v. Mauritius, in which the Committee concluded that, absent an explanation, the submission of the Communication after such a long delay must be considered an abuse of the right of submission. Consequently, no delay is acceptable without reasonable justification, and it is incumbent on the complainants who allege violations to act with due diligence in pursuing their cases. The Committee finds that the delay in submitting the Communication is not supported by reasonable justifications or tangible evidence.

Furthermore, as regards the allegation that the remedies are ineffective, the Committee takes up the reasoning of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the case of Anuak Justice Council v. Ethiopia, which concluded in its Decision on the Communication Minority Rights Group International and SOS-Esclaves on behalf of Sid Ould Salem and Yarg Ould Salem v. the Government of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania that a remedy is effective if it offers a prospect of success. If its success is not sufficiently certain, the remedy cannot meet the requirements of availability and effectiveness. Moreover, a remedy is considered sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint. The Committee notes that it appears from the file that the Respondent State provided copies of the judgments delivered by domestic courts. The Committee notes that these remedies succeeded in redressing the grievances of children who were victims of forced marriage and consequently concludes that there exist local remedies that the victims and the Complainants of the present Communication had to exhaust before seizing it. The Committee notes, however, that the 12 HRC, Communication 767/1997, Mr. Vishwadeo Gobin v. Mauritius, Decided at the 72nd session, 16 July 2001, CCPR/C/72/D/787/1997, para 6.3. 13 ACERWC, Legal and Human Rights Center and Center for Reproductive Rights v. United Republic of Tanzania, para29, ACHPR, Communications 147/95 and 149/96, Sir Dawda K Jawara v The Gambia, (May 2000), para 31 14 ACERWC, Communication no 007/com/003/2015, Minority Rights Group International and SOS-Esclaves on behalf of Sid Ould Salem and Yarg Ould Salem v. the Government of the Islamic Republic of Mauritania, Para 23. arguments of the Complainants, which concern above all the ineffectiveness of these local remedies and their capacity to redress the alleged violations, are unfounded and are not supported by evidence.

In any event, as regards proof of the exhaustion of local remedies, the Committee considers that it was incumbent on the victims and their representatives to ensure that they had all the relevant facts and arguments in order to prove the exhaustion of local remedies. The exhaustion of local remedies is a requirement of international law and not a matter of choice. The fact that they did not try to exhaust local remedies before seizing it, but only years after the alleged facts occurred, does not relieve the applicants of the obligation to exhaust the available local remedies.

According to the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the case of Diakité v. Mali, the burden of proving the exhaustion of local remedies rests on the applicants, who must provide proof that they have taken all the necessary steps to exhaust or attempt to exhaust all the local remedies made available to them, and it is not sufficient for the complainant to cast doubt on the effectiveness of the State’s local remedies on the basis of isolated incidents. Moreover, the complainants must attach all relevant evidence attesting to the measures taken to exhaust local remedies, or even proof of an attempt to exhaust local remedies.

According to the European Court of Human Rights in the case of SCOPPOLA v. Italy, under the “generally recognised principles of international law”, certain special circumstances may dispense the applicant from the obligation to exhaust the local remedies available to him or her. However, the mere fact of harbouring doubts as to the prospects of success of a given remedy, which is not obviously doomed to fail, is not a valid reason to justify the non-use of local remedies.

The same reasoning was adopted by the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the case of Mango and Others v. Tanzania, in which it concluded that “[t]he Applicants could have seized the High Court […] and that they should not have casually (sic) disregarded the remedies available in the Respondent State without even attempting to pursue them”.

The Committee notes that the present Communication contains no information on the actions taken before domestic courts by the Complainants with a view to putting an end to the alleged violations. Nevertheless, the Committee, noting that it is important to stress that none of the ten victims or their representatives raised 15 ACERWC, Communication No. 010/Com/003/2016, Mr. and Mrs. Elogo Menye and Rev. Daniel Ezo’o Ayo Represeted by Etoungou Nko’o Law Firm v. Republic of Cameroon, para 24. 16 AfCHPR, Case of Peter Joseph Chacha v. Tanzania no 003/2012, 28 March 2014, para 142. 17 AfCHPR, Diakité v. Mali, no 009/2016, 28 September 2017, (2017) 2 RJCA 122, para. 53. 18 See Anuak Justice Council v. Ethiopia Communication no. 299/2005, para 48. 19 ECtHR, Case of SCOPPOLA v. ITALY (No 2) (Application no 10249/03) Judgment 2009 para 70. a single action of their own before seizing it, concludes that the Complainants anticipated the ineffectiveness of the local remedy by merely expressing doubts without attempting to exhaust any remedy at the local level. Consequently, the Committee concludes that the present Communication does not meet the admissibility requirement set out in Section IX(1)(D).

On the basis of the above arguments and analysis, the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child notes and concludes that the Communication submitted by the author does not meet the admissibility requirements; the Complainants not having exhausted local remedies.
The Communication is therefore declared inadmissible. Adopted at the 39th Ordinary Session of the ACERWC held virtually from 21 March to 1 April 2022.

The Secretariat of the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Committee/ACERWC) received a communication dated 24 June 2020 pursuant to Article 44(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Charter/ACRWC). The Communication was submitted by the African Centre for Justice and Peace Studies (ACJPS) (the Complainant) on behalf of Umjumah Osman Mohamed. According to Section IX (2) (i) of the Revised Guidelines on Consideration of Communications by the ACERWC (the Revised Communication Guidelines), the Committee transmitted a copy of the Communication to the Respondent State party on 16 July 2020. The State Party submitted its response in December 2020.

During its 37 Ordinary Session held on 15-26 March 2021, the Committee considered the admissibility of the Communication and following the deliberation on the requirements of admissibility, the Committee declared that the Communication is admissible. The ruling was forwarded to the parties on 14 July 2021 (Ref: ACE/OL/10/185.21) and the Respondent was advised to submit its argument on the merits within 60 days. The Respondent did not submit its arguments on merits within the 60 days and further Note Verbals dated 06 September 2021 (Ref: ACE/OL/222.21) and 12 October 2021 (Ref: ACE/OL/10/240.21) was forwarded, reminding the Respondent to submit the arguments on merits to enable the Committee to deliberate on the hearing during its 38 Ordinary Session on the 15 to the 26 of November 2021. The Respondent did not submit the arguments on merits and other Note Verbals were sent to the Respondent (ACE/OL/10/007.22; ACE/OL/10/083.22; ACE/OL/10/308.22; ACE/OL/10/389.22) dated 20 January 2022, 28 February 2022; 15 September 2022; and 2 November 2022 respectively; reminding the Respondent to submit the arguments on merits. Despite these efforts, the Committee did not receive a response from the Respondent, hence the decision to proceed considering the question of the merits without the response and presence of the Respondent State in terms of section XII (1) of the Revised Communication Guidelines.

Umjumah Osman Mohamed is a Sudanese national born on 6 June 2000 in Khashm el Girba town in Kassala State, Eastern Sudan. It is alleged that in 2016, Umjumah Osman Mohamed was raped by Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud, an adult who also resides in Khashm el Girba town in Kassala state, Eastern Sudan. As a result of the rape, Umjumah Osman Mohamed got pregnant. It is further submitted that the matter was reported by the Umjumah Osman Mohamed’s father, Mr. Osman Mohamed on 31 August 2016 at Khashm el Girba police station.

The Complainant alleges that investigations were carried out by the Prosecution Attorneys Bureau and the case was referred to the Child Court since Umjumah Osman Mohamed was 16 years at the time of the alleged offence.

The Communication alleges that on 20 September 2017, the case was heard before the Child Court and Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud was convicted for rape and sexual abuse of a child under Article 45(b) and (c) of the Child Act 2010 respectively. It is alleged that he was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment and a fine of 20 thousand Sudanese pounds.

It is submitted that in 2017 Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud appealed against his conviction to the Appeal Court under Appeal Case Number 9 of 2017 and on 29 October 2017, the Appeal Court passed a ruling where it upheld the decision of the Child Court.

The Complainant indicates that Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud appealed against the decision of the Appeal Court to the High Court in 2018 under case number 12 of 2018. It is alleged that the High Court overturned the decision of the previous courts and acquitted Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud of rape on grounds that Umjumah Osman Mohamed is not a child in accordance with the definition in Article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 which states that an adult is a person whose puberty has been established by definite natural features and has completed fifteen years of age and whoever attains eighteen years of age is an adult even if the features of puberty do not appear. The Complainant alleges that the court used an ambiguous determination of childhood as ‘attainment of puberty’ in accordance with Article 3 of Sudan’s Criminal Act 1991 to rule that Umjumah Osman Mohamed is not a child thus, her case should not have been heard by the Child Court.

It is alleged that the High Court further held that being an adult who understood the sexual act, both Umjumah Osman Mohamed and Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud should instead be tried for the offence of adultery (zina) under Section 145(1) (a) of the Criminal Act 1991 by the Criminal Court. It is further alleged that the High Court also directed the Criminal Court to grant bail to Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud pending his trial for adultery.

The Communication alleges that the Complainant filed for a review of the decision of the High Court by the High Court Review Chamber and in 2019 the High Court Review Chamber approved the ruling of the High Court stating that it is in line with Sudanese and Sharia law.

It is alleged that thereafter, the Complainant petitioned before the Constitutional Court to annul the decision of the High Court on grounds that it was unconstitutional because it violates Article 27(1) and 31 of the 2005 National Interim Constitution, and it was contrary to Article 4 of the Child Act 2010 which defines a child as a person below the age of 18. The Complainant alleges that on 11 December 2019, the Constitutional Court in its ruling agreed with the decision of the High Court and dismissed the petition. It is further alleged that the Constitutional Court held that the decision of the High Court was in line with the Sudanese legislation and the 2005 Interim National Constitution.

It is alleged that Umjumah Osman Mohamed is thus currently awaiting trial for the crime of adultery before the Criminal court. The Complainant alleges that since pregnancy is conclusive proof of adultery under Article 62 of the Evidence Act 1994, Umjumah Osman Mohamed will be convicted and eventually subjected to 100 lashes pursuant to Article 145 of the Criminal Act 1991. The Complainant alleges that pregnancy rebuts the legal and constitutional presumption of innocence and immediately shifts the burden of proof to Umjumah Osman Mohamed to prove her innocence.

Based on these facts, the Complainant alleges that the Republic of Sudan has violated the rights guaranteed under the Charter, particularly article 1, 2, 3, and 16 as well as rights guaranteed under the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, particularly article 3,5, and 7.

The Complainant submits that the Communication fulfils the requirement of admissibility under Section IX (1) of the Revised Communications Guidelines. The Complainant focuses on all the requirements in section IX (1) of the Revised Communication Guidelines.

The Complainant submits that the Communication is brought in conformity with the provisions of the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. The Complainant submits that the Communication alleges specific provisions of the Charter that have been violated by the Republic of Sudan and which Sudan has undertaken to respect by virtue of articles 3 (h) and 4 (m) of the Constitutive Act.

The Complainant further submits that the Communication is not exclusively based on information obtained from the media. The Complainant submits that the information contained in the Communication is supported by unofficial translations of the laws of Sudan, the 2019 Constitutional Charter for the Transitionary period, the decision of the High Court and the petition submitted to the Sudanese Constitutional Court.

The Complainant further submits that the Communication is not before any other investigation, procedure or international human rights mechanism. Further, the question of violation of Umjumah Osman Mohamed’s rights has not been submitted to any other international tribunal or adjudicating body for determination.

The Complainant submits that all the local remedies available have been exhausted. The Complainant submits that after the High Court over-turned the decision of the Child Court and the Appeal Court, the Complainant applied for a review of the decision of the High Court by the High Court Review Chamber. In 2019, the High Court Review Chamber passed a ruling that agreed with the High Court. Thereafter, the Complainant petitioned the Constitutional Court to hold the decision of the High Court unconstitutional. Unfortunately, on 11 December 2019, the Constitutional Court passed a judgment that the decision of the High Court is constitutional.

Furthermore, the Complainant submits that the Communication is presented within a reasonable period after the exhaustion of local remedies. The Complainant submits that after the High Court (Kassala and Red Sea Chamber) overturned the decision of the Appeal Court, the Complainant filed for a review of the decision of the High Court by the High Court Review Chamber in 2017. The High Court Review Chamber upheld the decision of the High Court and thereafter, the Complainant lodged a Constitutional petition to have the decision of the High Court pronounced unconstitutional on grounds that it deprived Umjumah Osman Mohamed of protections granted to a child under Article 4 of the Child Act 2010. On 11 December 2019, the Constitutional Court dismissed the petition on the grounds that the ruling of the High Court was in line with the Constitution and Sudanese law.

Lastly, the Complainant submits that the wording used in the Communication is not offensive. The Complainant submits that the Communication has not been cast in any offensive language or suggests any offensive language and the language used was carefully chosen, and the document deals with legal arguments rather than political motives.
Based on these submissions, the Complainant seeks that the Communication be declared admissible.

In its response to the Complainant’s arguments on the Communication's admissibility, the Respondent State submits that the Communication is not admissible as it does not fulfil the conditions listed below under the Revised Communication Guidelines. The Respondent State’s arguments are based on three issues.

Firstly, the Respondent State submits that the Communication is not compatible with the provisions of the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Children’s Charter. The Respondent State argues that there is an emphasis on the support of all African Union Institutions to the Member States without intervention in the internal affairs of such States and without interfering with the administration of justice. In that regard, the Respondent State argues that Umjumah Osman Mohamed’s incident is an isolated individual incident that has not been repeated in such a large and systematic manner to render a violation that obligates the State to assume the stance of the defender of committing or the recurrence of such violations. The Respondent State further argues that the case is still pending before the national courts and has not been finalised; therefore, the submission of the Communication should be deemed as a blatant interference in the provisions, measures and procedures of the domestic judiciary and is contrary to the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

Secondly, the Respondent State submits that the Communication does not satisfy the requirement that a Communication should not raise cases pending before another international body. The Respondent State argues that the case is pending before the Criminal Court in the city of Khashm el Girba hence the Complainant’s actions in taking fear as a reason to resort to international institutions is unwarranted. The Respondent State further submits that no final decision was issued on the case, no appeal of the final decision was filed, and the decision has not become res judicata yet. The Respondent State emphasizes that the decision of the Criminal Court has not been passed, and in any event, it may exonerate Umjumah Osman Mohamed or apply the provisions of the Child Act of 2010. The Respondent State, therefore, submits that the fear of the likelihood of the sentence of flogging being passed on Umjumah Osman Mohamed, notwithstanding the form of the decision of the Court that might exonerate her, according to the recently introduced Amendments to the Criminal Code abolishing the flogging penalty, renders such fears groundless.

Thirdly, the Respondent State submits that the Complainant has not exhausted all the local remedies. The Respondent State argues that the Communication does not indicate that the Complainant filed a complaint to the National Commission of Human Rights and no advisory decision was issued prior to its dissolution in September 2020, knowing that the Commission is an independent human rights entity that was established in accordance with the 2007 Paris Principles on establishing independent national human rights mechanism. The Respondent State submits that such a Commission is recognised by the African Union and United Nations and enjoys the status of an advisory mechanism by several similar mechanisms. The Respondent State further argues that the Complainant did not lodge a complaint to the General Grievances and Corrections Corporation established in Sudan as an internal remedy path to be resorted to after the exhaustion of other justice and judiciary mechanisms. The Respondent State submits that the General Grievances and Corrections Corporation is deemed a supervisory body monitoring the judiciary and justice institutions’ performance and their enforcement of the National Sudanese law and international and regional obligations of Sudan, in particular in the domain of human rights.
Based on these submissions, the Respondent State seeks that the Communication be dismissed for lack of fulfilling admissibility requirements.

In analysing the admissibility of the Communication, the Committee relies on article 44 of the Charter and the Revised Communication Guidelines. The provisions of article 44 of the Charter and Section I (1) of the Revised Communication Guidelines stipulate that ‘non-governmental organisations legally recognised by one or more of the Member States of the African Union or State Party to the Charter or the United Nations, among others can submit a Communication before the Committee.’ The Committee notes that ACPJS is a registered non- governmental organization working to monitor and promote respect for human rights and legal reform in Sudan and is making the application on behalf of a Sudanese national. Moreover, Sudan is a state party to the Charter as it ratified the Charter in 2008. Furthermore, in terms of Section I (4) (a) of the Revised Communication Guidelines, the Committee’s jurisdiction is determined by the victim’s age at the time of the alleged violation. Although Umjumah Osman Mohamed is 20 years old, the Committee notes that she was 16 at the time of the alleged violation. As such, the Committee holds that the Complainant has locus standi to submit the case.

The admissibility of a Communication is determined based on the conditions of admissibility provided under Section IX (1) of the Revised Communications Guidelines. Therefore, the Committee assesses whether or not the Communication meets those conditions. From the Complainant’s and the Respondent State’s submissions on admissibility, the Committee has identified three issues that require analysis namely; a) Whether or not the Communication is compatible with the provisions of the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Children’s Charter; b) Whether or not the Communication raises matters pending settlement by another international body; and c) Whether or not the Complainant has exhausted local remedies, and whether the Complainant should be exempted from exhausting local remedies.

Section IX (1) (a) of the Revised Communication Guidelines provides that a Communication is admissible if ‘it is compatible with the provisions of the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Children’s Charter.

The Respondent State has invoked the principle of non-intervention into the internal affairs of States and argues that the Communication does not meet this requirement. The Committee however acknowledges that ‘once a State commits itself to a treaty or its membership of an organisation, that act implies agreement to be bound by decisions from these institutions that are responsible for implementing and giving effect to the treaty.’ The Committee further acknowledges that ‘by ratifying the African Children’s Charter, states automatically accept the competence of the Committee to ‘receive’ individual and inter-state communications.’ Article 1 of the Charter places an obligation on Member States to recognise the rights, freedoms, and duties enshrined in the Charter, and by ratifying the Charter, the Respondent State bound itself to the provisions of the Charter, including this obligation. Further, the Respondent State bound itself to the mandate of the Committee to promote and protect the rights enshrined in the Charter provided in article 42 of the Charter. This also includes the mandate to receive Communications against Sudan, relating to matters covered by the Charter as stipulated in article 44 of the Charter.

The Committee notes that the principle of non-intervention is not absolute as it is subject to limitations and there are exceptions to the principle. Indeed, the Committee acknowledges that under international law, particularly article 2(7) of the Charter of the United Nations, the principle ‘concerns the duty not to intervene in matters within the domestic jurisdiction of any State’, and this implies that States should be given an opportunity to redress violations within their own system. However, in the report of the UN Secretary General ‘In Larger Freedom: Towards Development, Security and Human Rights for All’, the Secretary General, while acknowledging that the responsibility to protect citizens lies first and foremost with each individual state, stressed that ‘ if national authorities are unable or unwilling to protect their citizens, then the responsibility shifts to the international community to use diplomatic, humanitarian, and other methods to help protect the human rights and wellbeing of civilian populations.’ Drawing from these sentiments, the Committee is of the view that the principle of non-intervention does not entirely preclude intervention and in the event that a particular state fails to redress violations in its own system, intervention is warranted.

The Committee notes from the Communication that the Respondent State was given an opportunity to remedy the alleged violations at the national courts but it is alleged that the Respondent State failed to do so. The Applicant has thus approached the Committee for redress and refusal by the Committee to deal with the matter on the basis of the principle of non-interference will be undermining the objectives and purpose of the Charter. While giving regard to the concept of State sovereignty and non-interference in terms of article 4(g) of the Constitutive Act, the Committee acknowledges that intervention is required in order to protect and promote children’s rights. The Respondent State cannot therefore seek to absolve itself from the obligations of the Charter by invoking the principle of non- interference.

The Committee notes that the substantive requirement of compatibility with the AU Constitutive Act and the Charter entails the necessity that complainants make reasonable claims that articles of the Charter have been violated. The Committee reiterates its decision in the Talibés case where it held that the condition of compatibility with the AU Constitutive Act and the Charter is met if a Communication alleges violations of the African Children’s Charter. The same was stated by the Committee in its admissibility ruling of Ahmed Bassiouny v Egypt, where the Committee held that in order to be accepted by the Committee, a communication should show prima facie violation of the provisions of the African Children’s Charter. The Committee notes that the present Communication alleges violation of specific provisions of the Charter (articles 1, 2, 3, and 16) and is therefore brought in conformity with the provisions of the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union.

In light of the above, the Committee notes that the Communication fulfils the requirements of section IX (1) (a) of the Revised Communication Guidelines on compatibility with the Constitutive Act and the Charter.

Section IX (1) (c) of the Revised Communication Guidelines provides that a Communication is admissible if it does not raise matters pending settlement or previously settled by another international body or procedure in accordance with any legal instruments of the African Union and principles of the United Nations Charter.

The Committee makes reference to its admissibility ruling in the case of Legal and Human Rights Center and Center for Reproductive Rights (on behalf of Tanzanian Girls) v Tanzania where it stated that the intention of this condition is to avoid subjecting States to similar international and regional judicial or quasi-judicial procedures on similar alleged violations. As stated in the same admissibility ruling, the Committee further acknowledges that a hierarchy should not be created among the various international judicial or quasi-judicial organs where one can appeal against the other. Furthermore, as held in the Committee’s admissibility ruling in the case Project Expedite Justice and others v Sudan, the Committee notes that ‘ such requirement is provided to prevent conflicting decisions and ensure efficiency of transnational tribunals.’

On the basis of this requirement and the Respondent’s State submission, the Committee notes that the key issue of determination in this Communication is the nature of the adjudicating body where the Respondent State alleges that the matter is pending. The provisions of section IX (1) (c) of the Revised Communication Guidelines are straightforward as they refer to matters pending before ‘international’ bodies or procedures and not ‘national’ bodies or procedures.

The Committee notes that the Sudanese Criminal Court is not an international body, hence the Respondent State’s argument is misplaced and would only affect the condition of exhaustion of local remedies, which the Committee will address in detail below.

The Committee notes that there is no other indication to the effect that the matters raised in the present Communication are pending settlement or have been previously settled by another international body or procedure in accordance with any legal instruments of the AU and principles of the UN Charter. In light of that, the Committee holds that the Communication fulfills the requirements of section IX (1) (c) of the Revised Communication Guidelines. the Complainant should be exempted from exhausting local remedies.

Section IX (1) (d) of the Revised Communication Guidelines provides that a Communication is admissible if submitted ‘after having exhausted available and accessible local remedies, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged or ineffective.’ As this Committee in the Children of Nubian descent case noted, ‘one of the main purposes of exhaustion of local remedies, which is also linked to the notion of state sovereignty, is to allow the Respondent State to be the first port of call to address alleged violations at the domestic level.’ Drawing from the Respondents State’s argument, the Committee will determine whether or not the Complainant has failed to exhaust local remedies by failing to submit the case to the National Human Rights Commission and the General Grievances and Corrections Corporation.

Drawing from its jurisprudence in the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) and Open Society Justice Initiative on behalf of children of Nubian descent in Kenya v The Government of Kenya (Children of Nubian descent case), the Committee reiterates that what is envisaged under the Revised Guidelines with regards to the exhaustion of local remedies is that ‘extra- ordinary remedies of a non-judicial nature do not fall within the notion of local remedies and need not necessarily be exhausted for a communication to be declared admissible.’ This position has also been adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights in the case of Cudjoe v Ghana where it was stated that the requirement of the rule of exhaustion of local remedies is that only ordinary judicial remedies need to be exhausted. The African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights in its jurisdiction and admissibility ruling in the case of Hamad Mohamed Lymbaka v the Republic of Tanzania, also held that an applicant is not compelled to exhaust remedies that are non-judicial in nature.

Judicial remedies can be understood as remedies that are ‘provided by independent tribunals on a non-discretionary basis according to law and provide remedies as a matter of right and in a binding and enforceable manner.’ As noted by the Human Rights Committee in the case of Brough v Australia, the Committee recognises that administrative bodies or National Human Rights Commissions that meet all of these standards may constitute appropriate domestic remedies as well. In the event that such bodies do not meet these standards, for example as a result of their issuing non-binding recommendations, or as a result of failure to issue their holdings according to clear legal rules, or due to other characteristics that give them a less-than judicial character, they do not constitute remedies that must be exhausted.

The Committee notes that the National Human Rights Commission of Sudan has a status of an advisory mechanism, while the General Grievances and Corrections Corporation is a supervisory body monitoring the judiciary and justice institutions’ performance and enforcement of the national laws as well as the international and regional obligations of Sudan. In that regard it is nited that these two bodies do not provide remedies that are binding and enforceable and are thus non-judicial in nature hence the Complainant cannot be compelled to approach these bodies.

The Committee notes from the alleged facts of the Communication that after the High Court overturned the decision of the Child Court and the Appeal Court, the Complainant approached the High Court Review Chamber and upon being disgruntled with the decision of the High Court Review Chamber, the Complainant approached the Constitutional Court. The Sudanese Constitutional Court is the custodian of the Constitution and is the highest court on matters dealing with the constitutionality of laws and provisions in accordance with the Constitution. In that regard, the Complainant exhausted all local remedies available.

Regarding the Respondent State’s argument that the matter is pending before the Criminal Court, the Committee notes that the Respondent State is referring to the adultery matter which is yet to be heard by the Criminal Court. The Committee notes that the subject matter of the present Communication is the decision of the High Court, the High Court Review Chamber, and the Constitutional Court of Sudan in respect of the rape matter, which decision is alleged, to have a bearing on Umjumah Osman Mohamed as she will be prosecuted for adultery before the Criminal Court. The Committee sees no reason why the Complainant should be expected to wait for Umjumah Osman Mohamed’s adultery trial which is a result of the decisions of the other courts, to be completed before approaching the Committee.

In light of that, the Committee holds that the Complainant exhausted all local remedies available and therefore the Communication fulfils the requirement of exhausting local remedies provided in section IX (1) (d) of the Revised Guidelines.
As to the other conditions of admissibility, the Committee does not observe any irregularity and no contention has been raised by any of the parties to the Communication.

On the basis of all the above arguments and analysis, during its 37 Ordinary Session which was held on 15 to 26 March 2021, the Committee concluded that the Communication fulfilled all the admissibility conditions laid down in the Committee’s Revised Guidelines on Consideration of Communications; and it accordingly declared the Communication admissible.

The Complainant’s allegations are based on the fact that whilst the Constitution and the Child Act 2010 define a child as anyone below 18, article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 defines a child as “a person whose puberty has been established by definite natural features and has completed fifteen years of age. Whoever attains eighteen years of age is an adult even if the features of puberty do not appear”. The Complainant argues that the interpretation of this Article has meant that children over the age of 15 have been treated as adults by Sudanese courts and denied protection granted to children under National laws and the ACRWC.

The Complainant argues that in accordance with Article 1 of the African’s Children’s Charter, the Respondent is under an obligation to adopt legislative or other measures as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the African Children’s Charter and this includes repealing Article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 and annulling any court decisions that rely on that provision. The Complainant submits that in as much as the Respondent State has enacted the Child Act 2010 in line with the African Children’s Charter in defining a child, Article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 remains unchanged and continues to be applied in the courts of law thus violating Article 1 of the African Children’s Charter. By declaring Article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 to be consistent with the Constitution, the Constitutional Court denied Umjumah Osman Mohamed protections she would have enjoyed as child in the Sudanese laws, the Charter and other International instruments to which Sudan is a state party.

The Complainant further argues that Umjumah Osman Mohamed has been discriminated on the basis of age as the High Court in its decision held that Umjumah Osman Mohamed is an adult who should not be tried in the Child Court but before the Criminal Court. The Complainant argues that denying Umjumah Osman Mohamed the right to be heard by the Child Court like any other child amounts to discrimination. Further the Complainant argues that the failure of the Respondent to protect Umjumah Osman Mohamed from sexual abuse and to effectively prosecute the perpetrator amounts to discrimination. Further, the presumption of zina on grounds of pregnancy by the High Court puts Umjumah Osman Mohamed in a disadvantageous position compared to Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud as Umjumah Osman Mohamed must bring evidence that (a) Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud committed zina and that (b) she committed zina without consent. Failure to prove either (a) or (b) means that Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud walks free from punishment, but Umjumah Osman Mohamed is still subject to 100 lashes.

Lastly, the Complainant argues that the decision of the High Court to acquit Mr. Tarig Idriss Daoud of rape and instead charge Umjumah Osman Mohamed with adultery amounted to failure by the Respondent to protect Umjumah Osman Mohamed from torture, inhuman and degrading treatment and sexual abuse, thus a violation of Article 16 of the Children’s Charter. It is argued that the Respondent State failed to ensure prosecution of the perpetrator when the High Court presumed consent by Umjumah Osman Mohamed (much as this was irrelevant under Article 3 of the Criminal Act 1991 because Umjumah Osman Mohamed was a child) on grounds that she had reached puberty and therefore was old enough to understand sexual intercourse. The High Court also failed to remedy Umjumah Osman Mohamed for the violation she suffered but instead directed for her to be prosecuted for adultery. The Complainant also argues that the corporal punishment that Umjumah Osman Mohamed will be subjected to after conviction for adultery also amounts to torture. vii. The Committee’s analysis on the merits of the alleged violations i. Alleged violation of article 1 on obligations of state parties
