Pour déterminer si le viol dont a été victime AS constitue une discrimination fondée sur le sexe, le Comité se réfère à sa jurisprudence. Dans sa décision sur la Communication présentée par l'Institut pour les Droits Humains et le Développement en Afrique et Finders Group Initiative au nom de TFA (une mineure) contre le Gouvernement de la République du Cameroun, le Comité a noté que la violence devient une violence fondée sur le genre lorsqu'elle est infligée à des femmes pour la seule raison qu'elles sont des femmes et le viol est l'une des formes de violence fondée sur le genre.

Dans le cas présent, AS a été abusée sexuellement et elle a été contaminée par une infection vaginale qui ne peut que contaminer les filles/femmes en raison de leur sexe. Malgré que AS a été abusée sexuellement et qu’elle souffre de l’infection vaginale qui ne peut que toucher les femmes/filles parce qu’elles sont des femmes/filles, elle n’a pas bénéficié de la protection prévue par l’article 3 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant. Le Comité note également que malgré que AS souffre de l’infection vaginale et que les troubles post-traumatiques s’observent sur la personne de AS en public qu’au milieu scolaire, cette dernière n'a pas bénéficié d’aucune forme de prise en charge que ce soit médicale, psychologique ou autre.

En outre, le Comité note que même si l'État défendeur n'est pas l'acteur qui a causé la violence basée sur le genre qui équivaut à une discrimination basée sur le genre et vu que l'État partie n'a pas fait preuve de diligence raisonnable pour prévenir, enquêter, poursuivre et punir efficacement Oumar Sacko ; ce manquement de l'État défendeur le rend responsable au regard des normes internationales des droits de l'Homme.

Dans le cadre de la présente Communication, le Comité note que l'État défendeur n'a pas pris de mesures nécessaires et appropriées pour protéger la victime contre le viol et garantir le soutien nécessaire à AS. Le Comité note également que l'État défendeur a violé l'article 3 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant en raison de son manquement à mener des enquêtes exhaustives et assurer la condamnation effective sur cet acte de discrimination à l’égard de AS, en l'occurrence le viol commis sur une mineure de 11 ans et la réparation effective du dommage subi par la victime.

Le Comité note que ce manquement de l’État défendeur de mettre en œuvre les mesures législatives de manière efficace, de prévenir le traitement discriminatoire infligé à AS ou de prendre autres mesures appropriées pour protéger AS contre toute forme de discrimination fondée sur le sexe constituent une violation de l’article 3 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant.

Les plaignants soutiennent qu’en prenant beaucoup de temps dans l’instruction du dossier de viol, la justice malienne n’a pas fait preuve de diligence pour l’intérêt supérieur de AS. Les plaignants soutiennent également que la procédure pénale telle que légalement prévue au Mali facilite que les juges d’instruction à tous les niveaux manquent d’instruire diligemment un crime et telle est le cas dans la présente affaire de viol.

L’article 4 (1) de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant prévoit que « dans toute action concernant un enfant, entreprise par une quelconque personne ou autorité, l'intérêt de supérieur de l'enfant sera la considération primordiale ».

L'Observation Générale Nº 14 du Comité sur les droits de l'enfant note que « les actions comprennent les omissions et les commissions qui se manifestent par des décisions, des propositions, des services, des procédures et d'autres mesures ». En outre, dans sa Communication soumise par le Centre pour les Droits Humains et la Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l’Homme contre le gouvernement du Sénégal, le Comité a indiqué que le principe de l'intérêt supérieur de l'enfant est applicable à toutes les actions ou omissions de la part de toute personne, y compris les acteurs étatiques et non étatiques. Ainsi, comme l’a noté dans sa Communication Minority Rights Group International et Sos-Esclaves au nom de Said Ould Salem et de Yarg Ould Salem contre le Gouvernement de la Mauritanie, le Comité a souligné que toutes les actions et inactions à l’égard des enfants ne doivent être que dans l’intérêt supérieur de l'enfant.

Le Comité note des arguments de l'État défendeur que le premier degré d’instruction s’est terminé en Mars 2020, 2 ans après la commission du viol sur une mineure de 11 ans. Le Comité note également que le deuxième degré d’instruction s’est achevé en Août 2020 ; et que c’est en Mars 2021 que la Cour d’Assises de Bamako a rendu une décision condamnant Oumar Sacko. En outre, le Comité note que l'État défendeur a uniquement jugé l’affaire sur l’action pénale et qu’aucune décision sur l’action civile n’a été prononcée jusqu’à ce jour. Dans ses arguments, l'État défendeur a indiqué que AS peut toujours demander l’enrôlement du dossier devant la Cour d’Assises ou présenter ce dossier devant une juridiction civile dans les délais de 20 ans que la Loi prévoit en matière civile pour demander à la Cour de condamner Oumar Sacko de lui payer les dommages et intérêts. Cependant, le Comité note que l'obligation de protéger et de garantir l'intérêt supérieur de l’enfant s'étend à l'adoption des mesures et des réponses rapides, adéquates et diligentes afin d’assurer la réparation effective des dommages. À cet égard, le Comité note que les procédures judiciaires dans lesquelles des enfants sont impliqués devraient tenir compte de l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant et être achevées le plus rapidement possible sans retard excessif. Le Comité note également que la procédure prévue par le Code de procédure pénale pour enquêter et juger les affaires de viol de mineure doit être conforme à l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant et répondre aux exigences d’une justice adaptée aux mineures victimes de viol.

Dans le cadre de la présente Communication, le Comité note que l’incapacité de l'État défendeur de mener des enquêtes en bonne et due forme afin de considérer l’âge exact de AS, victime de viol, lors de la détermination de la peine de Oumar Sacko; le fait de ne pas donner la possibilité à AS ou ses représentants de participer dans les processus judiciaires pour donner leurs avis sur cette affaire de viol jusqu’à prononcer une décision contre l’auteur du viol commis contre une mineure sans toutefois tenir compte de leurs demandes et le fait d’infliger une peine inférieure à la peine qui est prévue par la Loi malienne pour le cas de viol commis contre une mineure de 11 ans ne servent pas l'intérêt supérieur de l’enfant. En outre, le Comité note que le fait que la décision de la Cour d’Assises ne s’est pas prononcée sur les intérêts civils de la victime alors que cette dernière s’est constituée partie civile ne garantit pas la réparation du dommage causé à AS, ce qui est contraire au principe de l’intérêt supérieur de AS qui s’est constituée partie civile pour recevoir la réparation du dommage causé par le viol dont elle a subi.

De plus, le Comité note que l'intérêt supérieur de l'enfant comprend le court terme, le moyen terme et le long terme. À cet égard, le Comité note que l’État défendeur devrait tenir compte des effets physiques, psychologiques, sociales et émotionnelles entres autres nés du viol et de l'impact aggravé de l’infection vaginale que AS a contracté dans toutes les procédures judiciaires et administratives qu’il a entrepris. Le Comité note également que l’État défendeur devrait veiller à ce que AS soit au centre du processus de réparation en usant une approche de la réparation centrée sur AS qui devrait être guidée par une analyse et une pleine compréhension du préjudice subi et des souhaits de AS afin que la réparation fournie réponde et soit adaptée à ses besoins. Le Comité note qu’afin de respecter les exigences de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant quant à l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant, AS devrait jouer un rôle actif et participatif dans le processus judiciaire et de réparation.

Le Comité note également que l’État défendeur a posé plusieurs actions et omissions qui ne sont pas conformes à l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant notamment ; au cours du déroulement de la procédure interne, il s’est observé une lenteur dans l’instruction du dossier de viol et le manque de diligence raisonnable pour prévenir le viol et effectivement tenir compte des intérêts de AS ; la décision de la Cour d’Assises ne garantit pas ni la justice, ni la réparation effective du dommage subi par AS vu que cette dernière a été traitée comme une adulte et, ce qui a résulté en une sanction moins grave à l’encontre de l’auteur ; et, le système de protection de l’enfant n’a pas fourni aucune forme de prise en charge que ce soit médicale ou psychologique à AS depuis le moment des faits et le signalement du cas de viol à la police jusqu’à la décision de la Cour d’Assises. Le Comité note que pour l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant, la police devrait rapidement/automatiquement référer le cas de AS pour une prise en charge adéquate et holistique au niveau des services de prise en charge sans toutefois attendre que AS exprime le besoin d’être assistée. Tenant compte de ce qui s’est passé, le Comité note qu’il y a un dysfonctionnement du système de protection de l’enfant quant à l’orientation et le référencement des cas de violations des droits de l’enfant dans l’État Partie, ce qui ne garantit pas le respect du principe de l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant.

Par conséquent, le Comité estime que l'État défendeur a violé l'article 4 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant en n'accordant pas la priorité à l'intérêt supérieur de AS lors de l'enquête, la poursuite, la condamnation de l’auteur du viol (détermination de la peine infligée à Oumar Sacko) et la réparation effective du dommage causé à AS.

L’article 16 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant prévoit que les États parties doivent prendre des mesures législatives, administratives, sociales et éducatives spécifiques pour protéger l'enfant contre toute forme de tortures, traitements inhumains et dégradants, et en particulier toute forme d'atteinte ou d'abus physique ou mental, de négligence ou de mauvais traitements, y compris les sévices sexuels. Les mesures de protection prévues en vertu de l’article 16 comprennent des procédures effectives pour garantir la création d'organismes de surveillance spéciaux chargés de fournir à l'enfant et à ceux qui en ont la charge le soutien nécessaire ainsi que d'autres formes de mesures préventives, et pour la détection et le signalement des cas de négligences ou de mauvais traitements infligés à un enfant, l'engagement d'une procédure judiciaire et d'une enquête à ce sujet, le traitement du cas et son suivi.

Les plaignants soutiennent que le viol de AS qui a occasionné une infection sexuellement transmissible qui n’a pas encore guéri et des troubles post- traumatiques chez la victime constitue un traitement inhumain et dégradant contraire au prescrit de l’article 16 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien- être de l’Enfant. Les plaignants soutiennent également que le viol de AS a compromis, continue à compromettre la jouissance de ses droits et constitue un traitement inhumain ou dégradant à son égard qui a entrainé de graves conséquences sur la vie de la victime.

La question à examiner par le Comité concerne à déterminer si le viol commis contre AS constitue un traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant. Il est également nécessaire de déterminer si l'État peut être tenu responsable du comportement des acteurs privés, Oumar Sacko, dans le cadre de la présente communication.

Le Comité, pour déterminer si le viol constitue un traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant, s'inspire de sa jurisprudence et celle de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l’Homme et des Peuples. La Commission africaine a défini le traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant comme un traitement qui cause un préjudice y compris des dommages physiques ou psychologiques, par des actes ou des omissions qui constituent des violations des droits ; et, le viol a été cité parmi une des formes de traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant qui comprend des actes physiques et psychologiques commis contre la victime sans son consentement ou dans des circonstances coercitives. En outre, dans l'affaire International Pen et les autres contre le gouvernement du Nigéria, la Commission africaine a déclaré que les traitements inhumains et dégradants comprennent "non seulement les actes qui causent de graves souffrances physiques et psychologiques, mais qui humilient l'individu ou le forcent à agir contre sa volonté ou sa conscience. En l’espèce, le Comité note des faits allégués que AS souffre beaucoup au niveau physique et psychologique à cause du viol et de l’infection vaginale qu’elle a contracté. Le Comité note également des faits allégués que Oumar Sacko a commis un acte de pénétration par violence sur la mineure de 11 ans, ce qui constitue un traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant.

Ainsi, le Comité note qu’un acte commis par un particulier et qui n'est pas directement imputable à un État peut générer la responsabilité de l'État, non pas en raison de l'acte lui-même, mais en raison du manque de diligence raisonnable pour prévenir la violation ou pour ne pas avoir pris les mesures nécessaires pour fournir une réparation aux victimes. Dans la présente communication, AS, une mineure a été violée par Oumar Sacko, un acteur non étatique. Malgré les souffrances et l’infection vaginale que AS continue de subir, l'État défendeur n'a pas pris des mesures appropriées pour assurer effectivement et efficacement l’enquête et la poursuite de Oumar Sacko et une réparation effective à AS pour le dommage qu'elle a subi. Ainsi, le Comité sur la Convention contre la torture et autres traitements cruels, inhumains ou dégradants ou de punition souligne l'importance de la participation des victimes au processus de réparation et le droit effectif aux victimes d’obtenir réparation adéquate, efficace et complète et une indemnisation rapide, équitable et adéquate pour le préjudice qu’elles ont subi à cause des actes et omissions qui peuvent être attribués à l'État. Le Comité note que les victimes de traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant doivent accéder à une réparation et l'obtenir rapidement. Le fait de ne pas fournir un accès rapide à la réparation constitue un déni de réparation.

Le Comité doit examiner l'impact du viol, de l’infection vaginale et du manque de justice pour la mineure AS. Le Comité a précédemment déclaré que le viol est la pire forme d'abus sexuel et est gravement préjudiciable physiquement et psychologiquement aux enfants. Le Comité note que le fait que AS a été contaminée de l’infection vaginale dont elle souffre toujours, vu qu’elle n’a pas bénéficié des services de prise charge médicale et psychologique de la part de l’État défendeur et considérant qu’elle n’a pas encore eu justice pour le dommage qu’elle a subi ; constitue une continuation des traitements cruels, inhumains et dégradants nés du viol, de l’infection vaginale, du manque de justice et réparation effective du dommage subi. Le Comité note également que ceci est un traumatisme aggravé et supplémentaire pour AS, mineure et victime de viol qui n’a pas encore eu justice et réparation adéquate pour le préjudice subi. Le Comité note que le viol et le manque de justice et de réparation adéquate du préjudice que AS a subi présentent des obstacles majeurs qui l’empêche de jouir effectivement de ses droits et bien-être tels que prévus par la Charte africaine des enfants, ce qui constitue une continuation du traitement cruel, inhumain et dégradant et une violation de l'article 16 de la Charte.

En n'ayant pas réussi à prévenir, intervenir, poursuivre et à réparer de manière adéquate les sévices physiques et mentaux infligés à AS, l'État a violé son obligation de protection en vertu de l'article 16 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant, qui lui impose de prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour respecter, protéger, promouvoir et réaliser le droit de AS d'être libre de toute forme de traitement cruel, inhumain ou dégradant et notamment d'atteinte ou d'abus physique ou mental, de négligence ou de mauvais traitements, y compris les abus sexuels.

Le Comité note que les plaignants ont allégué des violations au titre des Articles 1, 2, 5 et 18(3) de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l’Homme et des Peuples (CADHP) et des Articles 2(1), 4(1) et 25 du Protocole à la CADHP relatif aux droits des femmes en Afrique (Protocole de Maputo).

Dans le cadre de l’exécution de son mandat de protection et promotion des droits de l’enfant, y compris lors de l’interprétation de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant et l’examen des Communications, entres autres ; le Comité note qu'il s'inspire d'autres traités et instruments internationaux relatifs aux droits de l'Homme adoptés par les Nations Unies et les pays africains. Cependant, en ce qui concerne les violations alléguées des articles de la CADHP et du Protocol de Maputo, le Comité prend note de la décision qu’il a déjà adoptée dans sa Communication soumise par African Centre of Justice and Peace Studies (ACJPS) and People’s Legal Aid Centre (Place) contre la République du Soudan où il a indiqué qu’il n'a pas le mandat de se prononcer sur les violations des instruments des droits de l’Homme autres que la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant.

Dans leur Communication, les plaignants ont demandé au Comité de condamner la République du Mali à payer une réparation monétaire forfaitaire de 50, 000, 000 de FCA pour le préjudice moral, physique et émotionnel né du viol et du manque de diligence dans l’instruction de l’affaire en plus des montants que débourse de temps en temps la mère de la victime pour la faire soigner. Dans sa décision sur la Communication soumise par l'institut pour les Droits Humains et le Développement en Afrique et Finders Group Initiative au nom de TFA (une mineure) contre la République du Cameroun, le Comité a indiqué que le viol cause un préjudice physique et mental profond et durable, qui entraîne, entre autres, une réparation sous la forme d'une compensation monétaire. En outre, le Comité note que l'indemnisation couvre, le cas échéant, le remboursement des frais médicaux et la mise à disposition de fonds pour couvrir les futurs services médicaux dont la victime aura besoin pour assurer une guérison aussi complète que possible ; les dommages matériels et immatériels résultant de l'atteinte à l'intégrité physique et mentale de la victime. Il convient de souligner que AS n'avait que 11 ans lorsqu'elle a été violée. En plus du viol qu’elle a subi, AS souffre d’une infection vaginale qu’elle a contractée lors du viol, des traumatismes et autres conséquences nées du viol. De plus, des signes de traumatisme physique et mental dû au viol que l’enfant a subi à un âge si tendre ne cessent de se manifester sur la personne de AS. Ces traumatismes empêchent l’enfant victime de jouir pleinement de ses droits et bien-être et risquent de l’affecter durant tout le reste de sa vie. Dans la présente Communication, AS n'a pas encore obtenu justice pour le dommage qu'elle a subi. Il importe de noter que malgré qu’AS souffre toujours de l’infection vaginale et des troubles post-traumatiques, elle n’a pas encore obtenu justice faute d’une décision judiciaire sur la réparation du dommage qu’elle a subi. Compte tenu de ces circonstances qui ne donnent aucun espoir à l’enfant qui continue de souffrir au niveau physique et psychologique, le Comité demande à la République du Mali de fournir à AS une compensation équitable pour le préjudice moral et physique qu’elle a subi en plus des montants que la mère de la victime est en train de débourser pour la faire soigner vu qu’après le viol la mineure a été contaminée par l’infection vaginale et continue à se faire soigner.

Pour toutes les raisons indiquées ci-dessus, le CAEDBE estime que la République du Mali a violé ses obligations en vertu de l'Article 1(1) (Obligations de l’État), Article 3 (non-discrimination), Article 4(1) (intérêt supérieur de l’enfant) et Article 16 (protection contre l’abus et la torture) de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant.

Le Comité Africain d'Experts sur les Droits et le Bien-être de l'Enfant recommande donc au gouvernement de la République du Mali de (d’) : a) Assurer immédiatement que Oumar Sacko soit effectivement poursuivi et puni pour avoir violé AS, une mineure de 11 ans et garantir une réparation effective du dommage subi par AS; b) Payer une compensation équitable à AS pour le préjudice moral, physique et émotionnel qu’elle a subi ; c) Demande à la République du Mali de réviser le Code de Procédure Pénale en vigueur quant aux dispositions relatives aux délais d’enquête par le juge d’instruction qui ne répond en aucune manière à l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant en cas de viol ;

d) Prendre des mesures pour évaluer la situation actuelle de AS et assurer, le plus rapidement possible, sa prise en charge médicale, psychologique et sociale pour qu’elle puisse faire face à l’infection qu’elle a contractée lors du viol, au traumatisme et à toutes les conséquences nées du viol ; e) Mettre en place une politique nationale d’assistance médico-psychologique des victimes du viol et créer des centres qui sont accessibles sur tout le territoire afin d’assurer l’expertise médicale (pour confirmer le viol), la prise en charge médicale et psychologique gratuite pour les victimes de viol ;

f) Travailler étroitement avec la société civile et les autres parties prenantes concernées pour élaborer et mener des programmes et des campagnes d'éducation et de sensibilisation à court, moyen et long terme en faveur de la population sur la prévention et la lutte contre le viol au Mali ; g) Élaborer des manuels de formation portant sur la lutte contre les violences sexuelles et basées sur le genre et conduire des formations à l’endroit des officiers de la police, le Ministère Public, les juges d’instruction et les juges du siège, entres autres sur les droits de l'enfant et les mesures de justice adaptées aux enfants afin de traiter de manière sensible et professionnelle les enfants qui interagissent avec le système de justice pénale, qu'ils soient suspects, accusés, plaignants ou témoins ;

h) Assurer la disponibilité d'une représentation légale, des travailleurs sociaux et des psychologues ayant une formation spécialisée et orientés vers les droits de l'enfant sur tout le territoire et prendre des mesures appropriées pour garantir la coordination effective des services de prise en charge pour effectivement assurer la prise en charge holistique des enfants, victimes de viol ; i) Fournir un soutien aux victimes à tous les stades de la procédure judiciaire ; identifier les causes et les conséquences de la violence sexuelle et basée sur le genre et prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour la prévenir et l'éradiquer ;

j) S'assurer que tous les organes du Gouvernement travaillent en collaboration pour mettre en place des programmes de réparation et recours efficaces, suffisants, accessibles et rapides et assurer la participation des enfants victimes à l'élaboration, l'adoption et la mise en œuvre de ces programmes ; k) Créer des numéros d'urgence nationaux gratuits, disponibles 24 heures sur 24, 7 jours sur 7, afin de permettre aux victimes ou à toute autre personne de signaler des cas de violence sexuelle, d'obtenir des informations sur la manière d'accéder aux services de protection et de soutien aux victimes et d'être orientées vers les services appropriés ;

l) Assurer la disponibilité et l’accessibilité des mécanismes d'alerte et de signalement des actes de violence sexuelle adaptés aux enfants sur l'ensemble du territoire, notamment dans les zones reculées et dans les principales langues et dialectes qui y sont parlés ; m) Veiller à ce que les représentants légaux qui s'occupent des enfants dans le système de justice fournissent à l'enfant toutes les informations nécessaires et le guident quant au déroulement et à la conduite de toute procédure ; n) Établir des mécanismes permettant d'enquêter et de poursuivre rapidement les violations des droits de l'enfant et créer des tribunaux spécialisés, reconnus par la Loi, en accord avec les principes d'une justice adaptée aux enfants, pour soutenir les principes et pratiques d'une justice adaptée aux enfants.

En l'absence de tribunaux spécialisés, veiller à ce que les tribunaux ordinaires soient habilités à adopter et à mettre en œuvre des procédures spécialisées pour les enfants et adaptées aux enfants. o) Veiller à ce que les lois et politiques de l’État Partie relatives aux enfants soient conformes aux dispositions de la CADBE, en particulier l’article 2 de la Charte Africaine des Droits et du Bien-être de l’Enfant. p) Conformément à la Section XXII (1) (i) des Directives révisées pour l'examen des Communications et le suivi de la mise en œuvre des Décisions par le CAEDBE, l’État partie à une Communication doit soumettre un rapport au Comité sur toutes les mesures prises pour mettre en œuvre la décision du Comité dans un délai de 180 jours à compter de la date de réception de la décision du Comité. Fait à Maseru, Royaume du Lesotho lors de la 40 Session Ordinaire 23 Novembre – 01 Décembre 2022 Hon.

The Secretariat of the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Committee/ACERWC) received a Communication pursuant to Article 44(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (the Charter/ACRWC). The Communication was submitted by the Association for the Progress and Defence of Women's Rights (APDF) and the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) on behalf of AS (a minor) (the Complainants) against the Republic of Mali (the Respondent State).

Upon receiving the Communication in accordance with Section III of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications, the Secretariat of the Committee conducted a preliminary review and registered the Communication under number: 0013/Com/001/2020. To facilitate the determination of admissibility, the Communication was duly transmitted to the Respondent State by Note Verbale, Ref.: DSA/ACE/64/76.20 dated 29 January 2020, in accordance with Section IX(2) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications.

Upon receipt of the Communication, the State Party should have submitted its response within 60 days from the date (29 January 2020) of the Secretariat's request. As the Committee had not received a response from the Government, two Notes Verbales (Ref.: DSA/ACE/64/128.20 of 22 June 2020 and Ref.: DSA/ACE/64/369.20 of 23 September 2020) were sent as reminders to the State Party to submit its arguments on the admissibility of the Communication. Despite these efforts, the Committee received no response from the Government. Consequently, and in accordance with the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications, and taking into account the gravity and sensitivity of the Complainants' allegations, the Committee decided at its 36th Ordinary Session held from 23 November to 4 December 2020 to proceed to examine the admissibility of the Communication without a response from the Respondent State.

During its 37th Ordinary Session held from 15 to 26 March 2021, the Committee decided that the Communication is admissible. The decision on the admissibility of the Communication was transmitted to both parties on 26 July 2021 and the Republic of Mali was invited to submit its arguments on the merits of the Communication within 60 days. The Republic of Mali, however, did not submit a response. Thus, at its 38th Ordinary Session (15-26 November 2021), the ACERWC decided to proceed with the hearing of the Complainants during the 39th Ordinary Session held from 21 March to 1 April 2022. (The hearing on the merits of the Communication was scheduled for 31 March 2022.)

On 29 March 2022, two days before the hearing on the merits of the Communication, the Respondent State reacted to the Communication for the first time by submitting its statement of defence. The Secretariat of the Committee forwarded the Respondent State's observations to the Complainants on the same day (29 March 2022).

Upon receipt of the Respondent State's observations (dated 30 March 2022), the Complainants requested a postponement of the hearing scheduled for 31 March 2022 in order to consult and submit an appropriate response to the arguments submitted by the Respondent State. On 31 March 2022, the Committee decided to postpone the hearing on the merits of the Communication to its 40th Ordinary Session and invited the Complainants to respond to the Respondent State's arguments.

On 31 May 2022, the Complainants submitted their response to the arguments of the Respondent State. And, during the 40th Ordinary Session of the Committee held from 23 November to 1 December 2022, the Respondent State and the Complainant party responded to the Committee's invitation to participate in the hearing on the merits of the Communication, which was held in Maseru, Kingdom of Lesotho. The Complainants and the Respondent State made oral presentations of their respective claims and arguments, and the hearing shed light on the arguments and claims of both parties.

In their Communication filed with the Committee, the Complainants report that an 11-year-old girl named AS was raped by Cheik Oumar Sacko, a 36-year-old man, while she was on her way to the market on 29 March 2018. After a long conversation with AS, Cheik Oumar Sacko forced the girl to follow him into a room inside an unfinished compound. Holding her by the throat, Cheik Oumar Sacko threatened AS with death and forced her to undress. Cheik Oumar Sacko then raped AS.

According to the Complainants, AS cried for help and the neighbouring compounds heard her cries. The Complainants state that Cheik Oumar Sacko was caught by a crowd that came to rescue the victim and was taken to the Sebenikoro police station, where he confessed to his act. The Complainants report that the victim's family was immediately informed of what had happened to AS. Moreover, the Complainants report that AS's family and AS immediately went to the Sebenikoro police station. The police advised them to take AS to the Gabriel Touré University Hospital Centre in Media Koura for medical care. Relying on the results of the medical examination, which confirmed that AS had been raped, the police drew up a requisition for an expert (doctor) the same day for medical confirmation of the rape. According to the Complainants, AS contracted a vaginal infection from which she suffers to this day. In addition, the Complainants state that after the ultrasound at the University Hospital Centre, the doctor recommended that AS's family take her to a psychologist to assess the psychological consequences of the rape, but she was unable to do so for lack of financial means.

According to the Complainants, the Brigade responsible for the protection of morals and children at the Bamako Commercial Centre was also alerted by AS's brother. The latter advised him to seek social and legal assistance from an NGO; hence APDF was approached for social and legal assistance. At the same time, Cheick Oumar Sacko was placed in police custody by the Judicial Police, which, at the same time, began its investigations. The Complainants state that on 4 April 2018, the Judicial Police transmitted the file to the Public Prosecutor's Office and the case was registered under number RP 286.

According to the Complainants, after the investigations of the Public Prosecutor's Office, the file was transferred to the investigating judge of the Court of First Instance (TGI) in Commune IV of the Bamako District during the same month of April, and AS's mother was heard by that judge. The Complainants state that since that day, AS and her mother have never heard of any follow-up to the investigation.

The Complainants report that on 4 February 2019, the investigating chambers of the TGI in Commune IV of the Bamako District were seized by APDF's lawyer by a letter of constitution as civil party in this rape case, already known to the judicial authorities since 4 April 2018. The Complainants state that until then, the investigating judge had not yet taken any other investigative steps in this case.

According to the Complainants, AS suffers greatly physically from the vaginal infection she contracted during the rape. On the psychological level, post-traumatic symptoms are already observed in AS, both in public and at school, especially when her case is mentioned. The Complainants report that AS is now afraid even to leave her parents' home.

The Complainants allege that, on account of the above-mentioned facts and taking into account the slowness of the proceedings before the investigating judge, the Republic of Mali has violated and continues to violate Articles 1(1), 3, 4(1) and 16 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC); Articles 1, 2, 5 and 18(3) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR); and Articles 2(1), 4(1) and 25 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa.

On the basis of the allegations, the Complainants request the Committee, among other things, to find that: The admissibility requirement relating to the exhaustion of local remedies is satisfied on an exceptional basis, as the existing remedies in Mali are unduly prolonged. Order the Republic of Mali to revise the Code of Criminal Procedure in force with regard to the provisions relating to the time limits for investigation by the investigating judge, which in no way meet the best interests of the child in cases of rape. Ensure, as soon as possible, the medical and social care of AS so that she can cope with the infection she contracted during the rape, the trauma and all the consequences arising from the rape.

The analysis of the admissibility of a Communication by the Committee is guided by Article 44 of the Charter and the Revised Guidelines on Communications. The Committee notes that the present Communication is submitted under Article 44 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, which allows the Committee to receive and consider complaints from "any person, group or non-governmental organization recognized by the Organization of African Unity, by a Member State, or the United Nations on matters covered by this Charter". The Complainants alleged that they have standing to submit the Communication as recognized non-governmental organizations. The Complainants also pointed out that the present Communication is submitted against a State Party to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, noting that the Republic of Mali ratified the ACRWC on 3 June 1998, and within whose jurisdiction the alleged violations of the rights set out in the Charter are said to have been committed.

The Committee also notes that the Association for the Progress and Defence of Women's Rights (APDF) and the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA) are duly registered in the Republic of Mali and in The Gambia, with the physical addresses of APDF: Hamdallaye ACI 2000, Rue 374-Porte 406 behind the ORCA shop, Bamako, Mali; and IHRDA: 949 Brusubi Layout, AU Summit Highway, Banjul, The Gambia, respectively. In addition, it should also be noted that the Communication is submitted on matters covered by the ACRWC. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Complainants have the capacity to submit a Communication in accordance with Article 44 of the Charter.

Furthermore, the Committee notes that under Section II of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications, a Communication filed in accordance with Article 44 is subject to requirements relating to the author of the Communication, form and content. The Committee analysed the present Communication to determine whether it complies with these requirements.

Section I(1)(c) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications provides that a Communication may be submitted by "any intergovernmental or non-governmental organization legally recognized in one or more member States of the African Union, by a State Party to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child or by the United Nations". The Committee notes that the present Communication expressly indicates the names of the authors as non-governmental organizations recognized by member States of the African Union; and the complaint is submitted on behalf of a Malian child, AS, who resides in the Republic of Mali and whose rights set out in the Charter and other regional legal instruments, to which Mali is a State Party, have been violated on the territory of Mali by the Government of Mali. In addition, the Committee notes that the Complainants have succeeded in proving that the Communication is submitted in the best interests of the victim. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Complainants have complied with Section I(1) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications.

The Complainants submit that the present Communication meets the requirements as to form set out in Section II(2) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications, according to which a Communication may be considered by the Committee only if it is not anonymous, if it is written in one of the official languages of the Committee, if it concerns a State that is a signatory to the Charter and if it is duly signed by the complainant or his or her representatives. In this regard, the Committee notes that the authors of the Communication are known and that other important information concerning the authors of the Communication has been provided to the Committee. In addition, the Communication submitted is written in French, one of the working languages of the Committee, and is submitted against a State Party to the Charter. The Committee also notes that the Complainants affixed their signatures on the last page of the Communication. In this regard, the Committee is of the view that the Complainants have complied with the requirements as to form as set out in Section II(2) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications.

In analysing the admissibility of the Communication, the Committee assesses whether the substantive requirements provided for in Section IX(1) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications have been met.

Section IX(1)(a) of the Revised Guidelines provides that a Communication must be compatible with the provisions of the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the ACRWC. The Complainants submit that this requirement is met since the Communication is submitted to reinforce the objectives and principles of the Constitutive Act of the African Union (AU), the protection of the rights recognized by the Charter and the respect of the commitments made by the Republic of Mali when it ratified the Charter. The Committee notes that the Communication is compatible with the Constitutive Act of the AU and the Charter since it concerns violations of the rights recognized by the Charter and the respect of the commitments made by the Republic of Mali when it ratified the Charter. In this regard, the Committee reiterates its Decision in the matter of Centre for Human Rights (University of Pretoria) and Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l'Homme v. The Government of Senegal and notes that the requirement of compatibility with the Constitutive Act of the AU and the Charter is met if a Communication alleges violations of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. The Committee also refers to the Decision of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) in the matter of Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe, according to which, for the merits of Communications to be considered compatible with the instrument concerned, it suffices to show that the complainant invokes provisions of the instrument in question that are presumed to have been violated. The Committee notes that the present Communication alleges specific provisions of the Charter (Articles 1(1), 3, 4 and 16) that have been violated by the Republic of Mali and that Mali has undertaken to respect under Articles 3(h) and 4(m) of the Constitutive Act. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Communication satisfies the requirements of Section IX(1)(a) of the Revised Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications.

In accordance with Section IX(1)(b) of the Revised Guidelines, the Communication should not be exclusively based on information disseminated by the media. The Committee noted that the present Communication is based on the statement of the facts by the victim's mother. The Committee also notes that, according to the Communication and the documents annexed, the Communication is based on evidence provided by the Complainants. Consequently, the Committee is of the view that the Communication satisfies this requirement set out in Section IX(1)(b), as information disseminated by the media plays no role in this Communication.

In accordance with Section IX(1)(c) of the Guidelines on Communications, a Communication may not raise matters pending settlement or previously settled by another international body or procedure, in accordance with the legal instruments of the AU and the principles of the Charter of the United Nations. The Complainants state that the allegations in the present Communication are not and have never been the subject of litigation before any other regional or international judicial body. The Committee finds that the Communication under consideration does not raise matters pending or previously settled by another international body or procedure in accordance with the legal instruments of the African Union and the principles of the Charter of the United Nations. The Committee therefore finds that the Communication satisfies the requirements of Section IX(1)(c) of the Revised Guidelines.

The Committee also notes that it has examined the Communication in detail and has found that the Communication is presented in polite and respectful language, which makes it compatible with Section IX(1)(f) of the Revised Guidelines.

The Committee notes that Section IX(1)(d) of the Revised Guidelines on Communications provides that a Communication is admissible, inter alia, if it is submitted "after exhausting available and accessible local remedies, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged or ineffective". In deciding whether local remedies have been exhausted or whether the present Communication may be admissible notwithstanding the non-exhaustion of local remedies, the Committee analysed and, at the same time, examined in detail the written submissions of the Complainants, and provides a more detailed explanation below.

Before its analysis, the Committee notes that the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) indicated in the case of Article 19 v. Eritrea that the rule of exhaustion of local remedies presupposes: "(i) the existence of domestic procedures to deal with the complaint; (ii) the justiciability or otherwise, at the national level, of the subject matter of the complaint; (iii) the existence, under the municipal legal order, of provisions for redress of the type of wrong that is the subject of the complaint; and (iv) the availability of effective local remedies, that is, remedies sufficient or capable of redressing the wrong that is the subject of the complaint.

Moreover, as the Committee noted in the case of Children of Nubian Descent, "one of the main purposes of the exhaustion of local remedies, which is also linked to the notion of State sovereignty, is to enable the Respondent State to be the first forum to hear of the alleged violations at the national level". In addition, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights has also indicated that the State concerned must be made aware of a human rights violation in order to remedy that violation complained of by the Complainants before being called upon to account for these violations at the international or regional level. However, complainants may be exempted from exhausting local remedies if such remedy would be or is unduly prolonged.

In the present Communication, the Complainants invoke, as an exception to the exhaustion of local remedies, the undue prolongation that continues to characterise Malian criminal procedure as well as the ineffectiveness of the available remedies. Moreover, the Complainants allege that it is not normal, and above all not in the interest of justice for the minor child victim of rape, that the file, which has been in the hands of the investigating judge since 4 April 2018, has not yet been closed as regards the investigation and set down for trial and for the determination of compensation for the harm caused to the victim. The Complainants submit that the undue prolongation of criminal procedure in Mali is enshrined in the Code of Criminal Procedure, which grants the first investigating judge a period of up to three (3) years to conduct the investigation in criminal matters. Moreover, the investigation by the first investigating judge is still subject to appeal by the Public Prosecutor's Office before the Indictment Chamber within the Court of Appeal, which means that in criminal matters in Mali, the file must necessarily go through two levels of investigation.

The Complainants argue that in the context of the present Communication, even if the first investigating judge were to complete the investigation of the file, it would still have to be sent to the Attorney General at the Bamako Court of Appeal, who would seize the Indictment Chamber for a second investigation of the case. Furthermore, the Complainants allege that not only is the undue prolongation already attributable to the time taken by the first investigating judge, but it is also exacerbated by the referral to the second investigating judge at the Indictment Chamber, which risks taking as long as or longer than the time taken by the first investigating judge. The Complainants allege that under criminal procedure, this case of rape of a minor will, after the investigation by the second investigating judge, still have to be set down before the Assize Court after the committal order by the Indictment Chamber. The Complainants submit that it is also not certain that the Assize Court, once seized, could immediately hear AS's case, as it is not a permanent court in Mali and sits twice a year. In addition, the Complainants submit that such a procedure is not only very lengthy for the protection of the rights of the child, but also proves so ineffective that it cannot lead to justice for a minor victim (11 years old at the time of the rape) of a flagrant and admitted crime whose consequences AS is currently living with.

The Complainants are of the view that this procedure offers no chance of success in doing justice for AS, especially as in Mali, when the file is in the hands of the judicial authorities and a person has joined as civil party (which the victim's Counsel has already done), the remainder of the procedure is in the hands of the Public Prosecutor's Office, which exercises the public action.

The Complainants add that since the complainant party joined as civil party on 4 February 2019 for possible reparation of the harm she suffered and that until then nothing indicates that the investigation will be closed soon, the Complainants can only note that local remedies are unduly prolonged and rendered ineffective in finding a solution to the violations of AS's rights.

Following the Complainants' allegations relating to the exception to the exhaustion of local remedies, the Committee analyses whether the present Communication may benefit from this exception to the exhaustion of local remedies.

The Committee notes that the exception to the principle of exhaustion of local remedies is especially important for protecting the rights of the child and the best interests of the child. In addition, as the Committee indicated in the case of Children of Nubian Descent, "one year in the life of a child corresponds to almost six percent of his or her childhood". Thus, the Committee is of the view that the fact that the file has been with the investigating judge for more than two years to investigate a case of rape of a minor, whose perpetrator does not deny the facts, in no way guarantees the best interests of the child, who still suffers to this day from the infection she contracted during the rape. The Committee also notes that "the implementation and realization of children's rights in Africa are not matters to be postponed but matters that require immediate proactive attention and action".

Furthermore, the Committee refers to the rules established under international human rights law, which require that "only local remedies that are available, effective and sufficient must be exhausted". In Communications Nos. 147/95 and 149/96, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held that a remedy is considered available if the complainant can pursue it without impediment or if he or she can make use of it in the context of his or her case. Moreover, a remedy is deemed effective if it offers a prospect of success; and it is deemed sufficient if it is capable of redressing the subject of the complaint.

Moreover, the Committee notes that whether a remedy is unduly prolonged must be assessed in the particular circumstances of the victim's case. The Committee is of the view that exemptions from the exhaustion of local remedies are assessed on a case-by-case basis. The African Commission and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights have both indicated that the availability and effectiveness of a local remedy are assessed on a case-by-case basis. Moreover, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights has indicated that it has no strict rules for determining whether a case has suffered "unwarranted delay". To determine whether the local remedy has been unduly prolonged, it has indicated that it examines the circumstances of the case and carries out a case-by-case assessment to decide whether there has been unwarranted delay. In addition, to determine whether a criminal investigation has been conducted "promptly", the Commission takes into account a number of factors, such as the time that has elapsed since the crime was committed, whether the investigation has gone beyond the preliminary stage, the measures adopted by the authorities and the complexity of the case. The Committee notes that in the present Communication, the Republic of Mali has taken more than two and a half years without, however, providing any specific information on the progress of the investigation concerning a raped minor suffering from a vaginal infection, in order to clarify the facts and punish the perpetrator of this crime. The Committee is of the view that there has been an unwarranted delay in the taking of Decisions by the Malian judicial bodies concerning the reported events.

In the context of the present Communication, the Committee notes that, taking into account the time the investigating judge has taken since 4 April 2018 to investigate a case of rape of a minor in which the offender does not deny the facts; considering the time that has elapsed while the file remains with the first investigating judge and that there has been no follow-up to the investigation of the case; noting that the file must necessarily go through two levels of investigation and require that the case be investigated by a second investigating judge; and taking into account that AS continues to suffer the physical and psychological consequences of the rape of which she was a victim, the Committee concludes that this procedure in no way guarantees the best interests of the minor child victim of rape; and, consequently, the Committee concludes that the Complainants should no longer be required to wait for the investigation by the investigating judge, whose procedure has not proved to be any faster so far. The Committee notes that such practices prove that the local remedy is unduly prolonged, whereas the State has had more time to respond to this violation. The Committee notes that this remedy is unjustifiable and unduly prolonged, which makes it unsuitable for the Complainants to pursue it.
In light of these facts and arguments, and of the consistent jurisprudence, the Committee is of the view that the case should benefit from an exception to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies.

In accordance with Section IX(1)(e), the Communication should be filed within a reasonable time after the exhaustion of local remedies at the national level. The Committee is of the view that the Complainants have complied with this requirement since they filed the Communication with the Committee after having tried to obtain justice in Mali for more than two years, without success.

On the basis of all the above analyses, the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child notes and concludes that the Communication submitted by the authors fulfils the admissibility requirements as defined in the Committee's Guidelines on the Consideration of Communications.

For the foregoing reasons, the Committee finds that the present Communication is admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 44 of the Charter and Section IX(1) of the Revised Guidelines for the Consideration of Communications.

The Complainants presented their arguments on the alleged violations of Articles 1(1), 3, 4(1) and 16 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. The Complainants' arguments on the merits of the Communication are presented in detail in the Section reserved for the Committee's analysis on the merits of the alleged violations. In addition to the arguments submitted to the Committee on the merits of the Communication, the Complainants indicated that the judgment rendered by the Assize Court of Bamako has no bearing on the AS case pending before the Committee, because the alleged violations of AS's rights and the requests made by the Complainants in the initial Communication are not taken into account by the decision of the Assize Court. Moreover, the Complainants indicated that this judgment treats AS as an adult whereas the birth certificate proves that she was a minor at the time of the events.

The Respondent State indicated that, considering that a decision convicting Oumar Sacko was rendered by the Assize Court of Bamako, all the violations alleged by the Complainants are unfounded. As regards the civil interests of the victim, the Respondent State indicated that even though the victim did not appear at the hearing to put forward her claims before the Assize judge, she still has the possibility of asking the Court to order Oumar Sacko to pay her damages in reparation for the harm she suffered.

Following the arguments put forward by all the parties involved in the Communication, the Committee defined the following questions as subjects for deliberation and inquiry to inform its decision: - Whether the decision rendered by the Assize Court of Bamako responds to the Complainants' allegations and requests; - Whether the decision rendered by the Assize Court of Bamako meets the requirements of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child; - Whether AS was an adult or a minor at the time of the events and whether she is entitled to effective reparation for the harm she suffered
The Committee has examined and analysed the alleged violations as presented in the present Communication and the other documents provided to it by the Complainant party and the Respondent State.

The Complainants allege that the following rights of AS (a minor) were violated by the Republic of Mali: - Violation of Articles 1(1), 3, 4(1) and 16 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child; - Violation of Articles 1, 2, 5 and 18(3) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights; and, - Violation of Articles 2(1), 4(1) and 25 of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa.

In its arguments on the merits of the Communication presented during the hearing of the said Communication held during the 40th Ordinary Session of the Committee from 23 November to 1 December 2022, the Respondent State indicated that all the allegations made by the Complainant party on the merits of the Communication are unfounded.

Article 1(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child provides that Member States of the African Union (AU) recognize the rights, freedoms and duties enshrined in the Charter and undertake to take the necessary steps, in accordance with their Constitutional processes and with the provisions of the Charter, to adopt such legislative or other measures as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the African Children's Charter.

The Complainants submit that the fact that rape is punishable under the Criminal Code of Mali is not sufficient to prove that legislative measures have been adopted to protect Malian girls against sexual abuse such as rape.

Thus, the Respondent State indicated that in March 2021, that is, three years after the rape, the Assize Court of Bamako rendered a decision sentencing Oumar Sacko to 10 years of imprisonment with hard labour. However, the Complainants stated that the accused was found guilty of the rape of an adult whereas the extract of the victim's birth certificate proves that she was a minor. Thus, the Complainants submit that the Assize Court heard only the accused and the Public Prosecutor's Office; the victim and her representatives were never involved in the proceedings so as to give their views/opinions on this rape case before the Court deliberated and ruled on the decision convicting Oumar Sacko. The Complainants also stated that the judgment is likewise silent on the civil interests of the victim, although the latter had validly joined as civil party.

The Committee notes that, as a State Party to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, the Respondent State is obliged to take all appropriate measures to protect AS from sexual abuse, including rape. The Committee also notes that States must adopt the necessary legislative and other measures to act with due diligence to prevent acts of sexual violence committed by State and non-State actors, to investigate such acts, to prosecute and punish the perpetrators and to provide redress to victims. In the present case, the Committee's decision must therefore be based on the assessment of due diligence, more particularly, the assessment of the actions, practices and decisions undertaken by the Respondent State during all stages of the administrative or judicial proceedings aimed at giving justice and reparation to AS. In other words, the question is whether the Government of Mali took all reasonable precautions and measures to prevent AS from being raped, and to effectively investigate, prosecute, convict and redress the harm suffered by AS. Thus, the Committee refers to its jurisprudence, notably Communication No. 0012/Com/001/2019 submitted by Legal and Human Rights Centre and Centre for Reproductive Rights (on behalf of Tanzanian girls) v. United Republic of Tanzania, where it indicated that the due diligence of the Respondent State is assessed on the basis of the result it has achieved through the measures it has taken regarding the matter at issue.

Based on the arguments of the Complainants and the Respondent State, the Committee notes that it is important to analyse whether or not the Government of Mali acted with due diligence in discharging its obligations towards AS. The Committee notes that the Respondent State has taken legislative measures to protect minors against rape and has adopted policies aimed at ensuring the prevention and care of child victims of rights violations, notably the National Policy for the Promotion and Protection of the Child in Mali (adopted in 2014); the National Policy for the Protection of the Family and the National Gender Policy, among others. However, the Committee notes that despite the existence of legislative measures and policies aimed at protecting children against violations of their rights, the Respondent State did not take concrete and appropriate actions to prevent AS from being raped, and the measures it took did not enable AS to benefit from the effective protection of her rights and the care she needed.

Furthermore, in accordance with Article 1(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, the Committee wishes to point out that, in addition to legislative measures, States are obliged to take all other necessary measures, notably administrative and judicial measures, among others, with a view to protecting and promoting the rights and welfare of the child.

Thus, the Committee notes that, in order to strengthen the realization of children's rights, children must participate and be heard in all matters concerning them. Moreover, the ACRWC requires that in any judicial and administrative proceedings affecting a child, States must provide the opportunity for the views of the child to be heard either directly or through an impartial representative as a party to the proceedings. The ACRWC also requires that the views of the child be taken into consideration by the relevant authority. In its Guidelines on Child Participation, the Committee recognizes the participation of children both as a general principle of children's rights and as a right.

Moreover, in its General Comment No. 12 on the participation of children, the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child stipulates that in criminal proceedings, the right of the child to express his or her views freely on all matters affecting him or her must be fully respected and implemented at every stage of the juvenile justice process. Likewise, that Committee notes that the right of the child victim to be heard is also linked to the right to be informed about matters such as the possibility of benefiting from health services, psychological counselling and social assistance, the support mechanisms available to children who lodge a complaint or participate in an investigation and judicial proceedings, the existence of protection measures and the possibility of receiving reparation, among others.

It is important to note that if the right of the child to be heard is violated in judicial or administrative proceedings, the child must have access to appeal and complaint procedures that provide for remedies. In the context of this Communication, the Committee notes that, under the provisions of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, Aspiration 10 of Agenda 2040 for Africa's Children and the cardinal principle of children's participation in any action concerning them, the Assize Court of Bamako had the obligation to involve AS and her representatives in the trial in order to consider the views of AS, a victim of rape, before ruling on the conviction of Oumar Sacko.

The Committee notes that such a failure on the part of the Respondent State guarantees no possibility for the victim to participate in the trial to submit her views, which is not in conformity with the provisions of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and Aspiration 10 of Agenda 2040 for Africa's Children.

In addition, the Committee notes that the question of AS's age is very relevant in this rape case in that the age of the victim determines the sentence of the perpetrator of the rape. On the question of determining AS's age, the Committee draws on the jurisprudence which suggests that unless the State proves the contrary to the allegation, the Committee considers the Complainants' allegation to be true. The Committee notes that the Complainants provided a copy of an extract of a birth certificate indicating that AS was 11 years old at the time of the events, and they stated that in civil matters, the birth certificate is an authentic instrument that is conclusive until challenged as a forgery.

However, in its arguments, the Respondent State indicated that AS was 17 years old at the time of the events but did not provide any authentic instrument proving the contrary of what the Complainants had provided. Thus, the Committee notes that the burden is on the Respondent State to provide another authentic instrument proving the contrary, but to date, the State Party has not provided the Committee with any other instrument. In its arguments, the Respondent State stated that a sexual assault perpetrated against an 11-year-old minor does not have the same classification and does not receive the same treatment as a sexual assault perpetrated against a 17-year-old minor. In this regard, the Respondent State stated that if AS was 11 years old at the time of the events, the classification would have been paedophilia rather than rape of an adult and the sentence would have been even heavier than the one imposed on Oumar Sacko.

The Committee notes 25 Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC), General Comment No. 12 (2009): The right of the child to be heard, paragraph 57. 26 CRC, General Comment No. 12 (2009): The right of the child to be heard, paragraphs 64 and 47. 27 Bousroual v. Government of Algeria, Communication No. 1588/2007, CCPR/C/99/D/1588/2007, paragraph 9.4. with concern that even if AS was 17 years old at the time of the events, the Government of Mali, a State Party to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, had the obligation to treat AS as a child and not as an adult; because under the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, a child is defined as "every human being below the age of 18 years".

Furthermore, in its arguments, the Respondent State indicated that it would verify the authenticity of the extract of the birth certificate provided by the Complainants before the Committee. The Committee notes that the Respondent State received from the Committee, among others, the Notes Verbales dated 29 January 2020 (Ref.: DSA/ACE/64/76.20) and 22 June 2020 (Ref.: DSA/ACE/64/128.20) informing it of the existence of this Communication, and that all the necessary documents (including the copy of the extract of the birth certificate) concerning this Communication have been provided to it since January 2020. The Committee notes that the Respondent State did not act with due diligence to initiate its procedures to verify whether the extract of the birth certificate provided by the Complainants was false.

The Committee considers that it is not at the hearing of the said Communication, during the 40th Ordinary Session of the Committee held from 23 November to 1 December 2022, three (3) years after having been notified of the existence of the Communication and having received the birth certificate as an attachment, that the Respondent State should express the need to verify the authenticity of that document. Moreover, the Committee notes that during the hearing of the present Communication, the Respondent State indicated that where, following verifications, it appears that the victim was actually 11 years old at the time of the events, the Code of Criminal Procedure provides a remedy, namely review.

Thus, on the question of review, the Committee notes that time is an essential factor, especially in cases of rape, and that the implementation and realization of children's rights in Africa is not a matter to be postponed, but a matter that requires immediate proactive attention and action. The Committee notes that this review will delay justice for AS, a minor who still suffers from the physical and psychological consequences of the rape and who has already waited 5 years to obtain justice and reparation for the harm suffered, in vain.

Moreover, the Committee notes that in the case of M.C. v. Bulgaria, the European Court held that "States have a positive obligation (...) to enact criminal-law provisions effectively punishing rape and to apply them in practice through effective investigation and prosecution (...)". The case of Bousroual v. Government of Algeria also indicates that where violence has already occurred, Governments are obliged to conduct exhaustive investigations and to ensure that proportionate compensation is paid to victims. In addition, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights has indicated that States Parties must ensure that the reparation provided is appropriate to the particular circumstances of the 28 Article 2 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. 29 Decision on the Communication submitted by the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and Finders Group Initiative on behalf of TFA (a minor) v. the Republic of Cameroon, paragraph 56. 30 M.C. v. Government of Bulgaria, Application No. 39272/98, European Court of Human Rights, Judgment, 4 December 2003, paragraph 153. 31 Bousroual v. Government of Algeria, Communication No. 1588/2007, CCPR/C/99/D/1588/2007, paragraph 11. ACERWC, Decision on the Communication submitted by the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and Finders Group Initiative on behalf of TFA (a minor) v. the Republic of Cameroon, paragraph 47. victim and proportionate to the gravity of the harm suffered. The African Commission has also indicated that compensation must be fair, adequate and proportionate to the material, moral and other harm suffered. In this case of rape of an 11-year-old minor, the Committee notes that the Respondent State failed in its obligation to conduct exhaustive investigations in order to establish AS's exact age, to effectively prosecute and convict Oumar Sacko and to provide the victim with compensation proportionate to the harm suffered. The Committee notes that the decision of the Assize Court of Bamako, which treats AS as an adult, does not guarantee justice for AS and in no way responds to the Complainants' allegations and requests.

On the basis of the above grounds, the Committee concludes that the Respondent State did not exercise due diligence to prevent AS from being raped, nor did it exercise due diligence to effectively investigate, prosecute and punish Oumar Sacko.

Owing to the lack of due diligence to prevent AS from being raped, to effectively investigate, prosecute and punish Oumar Sacko and to ensure effective reparation for the harm suffered by AS, the Committee considers that the Respondent State has not fulfilled its obligation under Article 1(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child to take all necessary measures to respect, protect, promote and fulfil the rights listed in the Charter.

The Complainants submit that the rape perpetrated against AS, followed by a negligent investigation by the Malian justice system, constitutes sex-based treatment/violence and is therefore discrimination on the basis of the sex of the victim.

Article 3 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child stipulates that every child shall be entitled to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognized and guaranteed in the Charter irrespective of sex, among other grounds.

In order to determine whether the rape suffered by AS constitutes discrimination on the basis of sex, the Committee refers to its jurisprudence. In its decision on the Communication submitted by the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and Finders Group Initiative on behalf of TFA (a minor) v. the Government of the Republic of Cameroon, the Committee noted that violence becomes gender-based violence when it is inflicted on women for the sole reason that they are women, and rape is one of the forms of gender-based violence.

In the present case, AS was sexually abused and she contracted a vaginal infection which can only affect girls/women by reason of their sex. Despite the fact that AS was sexually abused and suffers from a vaginal infection which can only affect women/girls because they are women/girls, she did not benefit from the protection provided for by Article 3 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. The Committee also notes that although AS suffers from the vaginal infection and post-traumatic disorders are observed in AS both in public and at school, she has not benefited from any form of care, whether medical, psychological or other.

In addition, the Committee notes that even if the Respondent State is not the actor that caused the gender-based violence that amounts to gender-based discrimination, and given that the State Party failed to exercise due diligence to effectively prevent, investigate, prosecute and punish Oumar Sacko, this failure of the Respondent State makes it responsible under international human rights standards.

In the context of the present Communication, the Committee notes that the Respondent State did not take the necessary and appropriate measures to protect the victim against rape and to guarantee the necessary support to AS. The Committee also notes that the Respondent State violated Article 3 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child owing to its failure to conduct exhaustive investigations and to ensure the effective conviction for this act of discrimination against AS, in this case the rape committed against an 11-year-old minor, and the effective reparation of the harm suffered by the victim.

The Committee notes that this failure of the Respondent State to implement legislative measures effectively, to prevent the discriminatory treatment inflicted on AS or to take other appropriate measures to protect AS against any form of discrimination based on sex constitutes a violation of Article 3 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child.

The Complainants submit that, by taking a long time in the investigation of the rape file, the Malian justice system did not show diligence for the best interests of AS. The Complainants also submit that criminal procedure as legally provided for in Mali enables investigating judges at all levels to fail to investigate a crime diligently, as is the case in the present rape case.

Article 4(1) of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child provides that "in all actions concerning the child undertaken by any person or authority the best interests of the child shall be the primary consideration".

General Comment No. 14 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child notes that "actions include omissions and commissions, which are manifested in decisions, proposals, services, procedures and other measures". Moreover, in its Communication submitted by the Centre for Human Rights and Rencontre Africaine pour la Défense des Droits de l'Homme v. the Government of Senegal, the Committee indicated that the principle of the best interests of the child applies to all actions or omissions by any person, including State and non-State actors. Thus, as noted in its Communication Minority Rights Group International and SOS-Esclaves on behalf of Said Ould Salem and Yarg Ould Salem v. the Government of Mauritania, the Committee emphasised that all actions and inactions in respect of children must be solely in the best interests of the child.

The Committee notes from the arguments of the Respondent State that the first level of investigation ended in March 2020, 2 years after the commission of the rape of an 11-year-old minor. The Committee also notes that the second level of investigation was completed in August 2020; and that it was in March 2021 that the Assize Court of Bamako rendered a decision convicting Oumar Sacko. In addition, the Committee notes that the Respondent State tried the case only on the criminal action and that no decision on the civil action has been pronounced to date. In its arguments, the Respondent State indicated that AS may still request that the file be placed on the docket of the Assize Court or bring the case before a civil court within the 20-year time limit that the Law provides in civil matters, to ask the Court to order Oumar Sacko to pay her damages. However, the Committee notes that the obligation to protect and guarantee the best interests of the child extends to the adoption of prompt, adequate and diligent measures and responses in order to ensure effective reparation for harm. In this regard, the Committee notes that judicial proceedings in which children are involved should take into account the best interests of the child and be completed as quickly as possible without undue delay. The Committee also notes that the procedure provided for in the Code of Criminal Procedure for investigating and trying cases of rape of a minor must be consistent with the best interests of the child and meet the requirements of justice adapted to minor victims of rape.

In the context of the present Communication, the Committee notes that the following do not serve the best interests of the child: the failure of the Respondent State to conduct proper investigations in order to establish the exact age of AS, a victim of rape, when determining Oumar Sacko's sentence; the failure to give AS or her representatives the opportunity to participate in the judicial processes to give their views on this rape case, up to the pronouncement of a decision against the perpetrator of the rape committed against a minor, without taking their requests into account; and the imposition of a sentence lower than the one provided for by Malian Law for a case of rape committed against an 11-year-old minor. In addition, the Committee notes that the fact that the decision of the Assize Court did not rule on the civil interests of the victim, although the latter had joined as civil party, does not guarantee reparation for the harm caused to AS, which is contrary to the principle of the best interests of AS, who joined as civil party in order to receive reparation for the harm caused by the rape she suffered.

Moreover, the Committee notes that the best interests of the child encompass the short term, the medium term and the long term. In this regard, the Committee notes that the Respondent State should have taken into account the physical, psychological, social and emotional effects, among others, arising from the rape and the aggravated impact of the vaginal infection that AS contracted, in all the judicial and administrative proceedings it undertook. The Committee also notes that the Respondent State should ensure that AS is at the centre of the reparation process by using an AS-centred approach to reparation that should be guided by an analysis and full understanding of the harm suffered and of AS's wishes, so that the reparation provided responds to and is adapted to her needs. The Committee notes that, in order to comply with the requirements of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child as to the best interests of the child, AS should play an active and participatory role in the judicial and reparation process.
